meta.title: NIS2 MCP server: what it is and what it does
meta.description: A NIS2 MCP server lets your own AI assistant read and fill in the NIS2 walkthrough, as you. Finishing items and approving them stay with people in the app.

mcpServer.title: What is a NIS2 MCP server?
mcpServer.subtitle: An MCP server is the connection through which an AI assistant works with another program. The nisd2.eu server lets your own assistant, such as Claude or Copilot, read and fill in the NIS 2 walkthrough as the person who connected it. Finishing, deciding and approving stay with people, in the app.

sections.heading: What is an MCP server, in plain words?
paragraphs: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It is an open standard that lets an AI assistant use another program: it reads data there and calls functions.
The program offers an MCP server for this, and the assistant connects to it. Claude, ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot Studio can all add MCP servers today.

The nisd2.eu MCP server is that connection for the NIS 2 walkthrough. Through it your own assistant reads your items and fills in what they ask for, as the person who connected it, with exactly their rights.

sections.heading: What does the nisd2.eu MCP server do?
paragraphs: Every nisd2.eu instance serves its MCP server at /api/mcp, a self-hosted one too. On nisd2.eu the address is https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp.
It gives your assistant five tools. With get_walkthrough it reads your walkthrough. With fill_walkthrough_item it fills in, for example suppliers, software, ratings or the text of a policy.

With upload_file it uploads a file as evidence, if it can send files itself, as Claude Code can; send_supplier_questionnaire sends suppliers the questionnaire. With read_records, once an admin allows it, the assistant of someone who may export reads all of the company's records as the export holds them. Everything goes through the same checks as in the app.
If a person holds the Reviewer or Legal reviewer access role in the team, their assistant only reads. What an assistant fills in on which item, our article on that sets out item by item.

sections.heading: What may the assistant not do?
paragraphs: It finishes no item, decides none and signs nothing. The server has no tool for these steps, nor for deleting suppliers, assets or trainings, or for inviting colleagues.
Items already finished, recorded as deliberately not done, or signed it leaves alone.
Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2, management approves the measures. In the walkthrough it approves at item 7.3, with its own account. A managing director's assistant cannot do that either.

sections.heading: How is it different from other MCP servers on NIS 2?
paragraphs: Most MCP servers with NIS 2 in their name that we found in October 2026 are knowledge collections. They answer questions about the law, map requirements to each other or check a domain from the outside.
They do not know your company, and they write nothing into your records.
The nisd2.eu server works inside your walkthrough. It reads what your company has already recorded and writes into the lists your management approves at the end.

sections.heading: How do I get started?
paragraphs: The server is meant for companies that use the NIS 2 walkthrough and already use an AI assistant. It helps most where the facts already exist in another form, such as an accounts payable list or an inventory.
First an admin turns on “Allow AI assistants for this company” in Settings. You open Settings from the profile menu at the bottom of the left sidebar.

Then anyone whose account has the walkthrough unlocked connects their own assistant: enter the address, sign in through the browser, allow access. Where no browser is possible, they use “Create key” in Settings to get a key that is valid for 90 days.
We tested both ways with Claude Code: run the command below, type /mcp in Claude Code, sign in. We have not tested Claude on the web, ChatGPT, Copilot Studio or the other assistants ourselves yet.
sections.code: claude mcp add --transport http nisd2 https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp

sections.heading: Where do I find the guide for my assistant?
paragraphs: Articles of their own explain setup in Claude Code, in Claude on the web and desktop, in Copilot Studio, in ChatGPT, and in VS Code, Cursor or Gemini CLI. Others cover running it on a self-hosted instance, choosing between a key and the browser sign-in, and allowing and disconnecting assistants.

Security, data protection and prompt injection (instructions hidden in data) each have an article. Further ones cover whether AI can implement NIS 2 for you, who is liable for its entries and how you trace them.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: You see the assistant most clearly on the lists the walkthrough starts with.
points: 2.2 Write down what your company has: the assistant ticks what your inventory shows and records what each entry is exactly and who provides it. You check each list and finish.
5.1 Write down who works for you: it creates the suppliers from your accounts payable list. In the app you remove anything that is not a supplier.
Every screen an assistant wrote carries a mark such as “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”.
7.3 Record the management review: no assistant fills in anything here. A person records the management review in the app, and management approves.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 2.2, screen “Software for customers, staff and money”. At the top the mark “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”, below it the note that the entry “Warenwirtschaft (ERP)” is on your list.

items.q: Is an MCP server the same as an API?
items.a: Not quite. An API is an interface each program builds its own way. MCP sets out how an AI assistant finds and calls such tools, so it can use many programs in the same way. Behind the nisd2.eu MCP server are the same functions the app itself calls.

items.q: Is an MCP server an AI agent?
items.a: No. The server takes your assistant's calls, checks them and saves what the app would save. The AI is the assistant your company chose.

items.q: Is MCP an open standard?
items.a: Yes. In December 2025 Anthropic donated MCP to the Linux Foundation's new Agentic AI Foundation, which Anthropic, Block and OpenAI co-founded. If the assistant your company already uses can add MCP servers, connect that one.

items.q: Can several people on my team use the MCP server?
items.a: Yes, each with their own connection. An assistant always works as the person who connected it, with their rights. In Settings each person sees their connections and ends them one at a time with “Disconnect”, or all at once with “Disconnect all assistants”.

items.q: Does it work if we self-host nisd2.eu?
items.a: Yes, every instance has the server, and signing in needs no third-party service. Claude on the web, ChatGPT and Copilot Studio connect from their vendor's cloud, though, so your instance has to be reachable from the internet over https. Claude Code runs on your computer and also reaches an instance inside the company network.

meta.title: NIS2 with AI: what an AI agent can and cannot do
meta.description: Implementing NIS2 with AI: an AI agent gathers facts and enters them in the walkthrough. Your company carries out the measures, management approves them.

canAiImplement.title: Can you implement NIS2 with AI?
canAiImplement.subtitle: Partly. An AI assistant can collect facts, sort them, write them down and propose text. Your company carries out the measures, and management has to approve them (Art. 20(1) NIS 2). In the NIS 2 walkthrough a connected assistant fills in; people finish and approve.

sections.heading: What can an AI assistant take on for NIS 2?
paragraphs: It can gather facts that already exist and put them into the shape the walkthrough asks for. From an accounts payable list, an inventory or a licence overview it makes rows in a list.
For a policy it picks the sections that apply and writes what else holds in your company.
That is what the NIS 2 walkthrough is built for: it asks item by item what needs recording, and a connected assistant enters it there.

sections.heading: What does your company have to do itself?
paragraphs: A measure is in place when it works in daily operations: when, say, the second factor is switched on at the sign-ins and the backup can really be restored.
An assistant that fills in records can write this down. It cannot make it happen.
The decision stays with people too: under Art. 20(1) NIS 2, management approves the measures and oversees their implementation. Who is liable for what an AI enters, our article on that explains.

sections.heading: What does NIS 2 say about AI?
paragraphs: Little. The Directive names artificial intelligence in two recitals only, the reasoning that comes before the articles.

Under recital 51, Member States should encourage AI where it could improve the detection and prevention of cyberattacks, in line with data protection law. Under recital 89, entities should evaluate their own cybersecurity capabilities and, where appropriate, bring in technology such as AI or machine learning.

Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, which sets out the measures in more detail for certain digital services, does not mention AI at all. Neither text says whether a risk analysis may be produced with the help of AI.
No authority has said whether it accepts NIS 2 records written with AI, as far as we could check (as of October 2026).

sections.heading: Where does an assistant help in the NIS 2 walkthrough, and where not?
paragraphs: Most with lists that already exist in another form. In 2.2 your inventory becomes the list of your software and technology, in 5.1 your accounts payable list becomes the list of your suppliers.
It helps little with facts that are written down nowhere. If no document records when a backup was last restored successfully, the assistant cannot know it.
So the server instructs it to enter only what your records and systems show, and to leave a field empty rather than guess.
For two decisions it has no tool at all: whether your company decides not to do an item, and whether management approves the documents. People make those in the app.

sections.heading: What happens when the AI gets it wrong?
paragraphs: A language model can invent facts or put them in the wrong place. In the walkthrough that could be a supplier that does not exist, or a backup schedule that is wrong.
The server checks the form of an entry, for example that a date is a date. Whether it is true, it cannot know.
That is why a person finishes every item. Each screen an assistant wrote carries its name and the day. Read those screens before you finish, and correct in the app what is wrong.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: These items show where an assistant helps and where you decide.
points: 2.1 Decide how you rate risks: the assistant can adopt the proposed method. Read the explanation and the example matrix first, because the ratings in 2.3 rest on this method.
2.2 Write down what your company has: from your inventory it enters software, technology and providers. You check each list, remove in the app what is wrong, and finish.

The screen of every document, such as the security policy in 2.4, has the tick box “I have read the document, and it fits our company”. Only a person in the app can tick it, and the screen only lets them continue once it is ticked.
7.3 Record the management review: management approves the documents and signs off the items. No assistant has a tool for that.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 12.2, first step “Understand”: the explanation “Registering with your authority” in plain words, on the right the box “Often missed” and below it the provisions the item rests on, Art. 3 NIS 2 and § 33 Abs. 1 BSIG.
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, check it yourself

items.q: Is there an AI agent for NIS 2?
items.a: An AI agent is an assistant that calls tools itself. Your own assistant, such as Claude Code, works that way through the NIS 2 walkthrough's MCP server: it reads your items and fills in what they ask for. It cannot finish or approve.

items.q: Can AI fill in the whole walkthrough on its own?
items.a: No. It fills in fields, lists and texts, but a person finishes every item, and management approves at the end. In 7.3 it fills in nothing at all. What it enters should be checked by someone who knows your company.

items.q: Which AI assistant works for NIS 2?
items.a: One that can connect to an MCP server and asks before it changes data. So far we have tested Claude Code. For Claude on the web, Copilot Studio, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor and Gemini CLI there are guides of their own, following the vendors' documentation.

items.q: Does AI help with registering with the BSI?
items.a: In 12.2 an assistant can record what the registration produced: the user account ID of your organisation certificate and the date of registration. The registration itself happens in the BSI's portal, outside the walkthrough.

meta.title: Who is liable for AI entries under NIS2? What Art. 20 says
meta.description: Who is liable when AI enters data in the NIS2 walkthrough? Management approves and oversees under Art. 20 NIS 2. Why no assistant can approve anything.

accountability.title: Who is liable for AI entries under NIS2?
accountability.subtitle: Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2, management approves the measures, oversees their implementation and can be held liable for infringements, whoever filled in a field. In the walkthrough every entry an assistant makes stands under the name of the person who connected it. No assistant can finish or approve an item.

sections.heading: What does NIS 2 give to management?
sections.law: Art. 20(1) NIS 2 · § 38(1) BSIG · Annex point 2.1.1 CIR (EU) 2024/2690
paragraphs: Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2, management approves the risk management measures under Art. 21. It oversees their implementation and can be held liable for infringements.
In Germany, § 38(1) BSIG transposes this: management is obliged to implement the measures and oversee their implementation.

For certain digital services, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 goes further. Under point 2.1.1 of its Annex, management accepts the risk assessment results and the residual risks, or an accountable person who reports to it.
None of these provisions mentions AI. The duty to approve and oversee stays with management, whoever filled in a field.

sections.heading: Whose entry is it in the walkthrough?
paragraphs: In the walkthrough an assistant works as the person who connected it, with exactly their rights. What it saves appears in the activity log under that person's name, with “via” and the assistant's name.
So it is that person's entry. They connected the assistant and can disconnect it in Settings at any time.
With the switch “Allow AI assistants for this company” an admin can turn assistants off for the whole company. That ends every connection.

sections.heading: Why can the assistant not approve anything?
paragraphs: Approval belongs to management, so the MCP server has no tool for it. An assistant cannot finish an item, cannot record that the company decided not to do one, and cannot approve anything.

At 7.3 only someone who has been assigned the team role “CEO / Managing Director” can approve, signed in with their own account. The name and the date of the approval then stand on each document they approved.

sections.heading: What does the AI Act say?
paragraphs: A company that uses an AI assistant at work is its “deployer” under Art. 3(4) AI Act. Art. 4 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 asks deployers for measures that support the AI literacy of their staff, with no specific level required.
In our reading, not an authority's, filling in NIS 2 records is not a high-risk use under Annex III. Our article on NIS 2 and the AI Act covers this in more detail.

sections.heading: Does management have to understand what it approves?
paragraphs: Approving and overseeing assume that management understands what it decides on. Under Art. 20(2) NIS 2, members of management have to follow training.
In Germany, § 38(3) BSIG requires management to take part in training regularly.
In the walkthrough this is item 1.1. An assistant can record there who was trained when, and upload the certificate if it can send files itself. Management has to take part itself.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: In the walkthrough, accountability shows in two places: training at the start and approval at the end.
points: 1.1 Get management trained: an assistant records who in management was trained when. Management attends the training itself.
Before finishing each item, a person reads the screens that carry an assistant's mark and corrects in the app what is wrong.
7.3 Record the management review: management sees its risks and the open points, each with a record of who takes care of it and by when, and approves the documents. Name and date are recorded.
After that, the server refuses an assistant's change to a list a signed item rests on. A person makes such changes in the app, and the item goes back to management.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 7.3, screen “Management approves the documents”: the documents the walkthrough wrote, each marked “Approved on 3 October 2026 by Claudia Lohse”.
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, prepare approval

items.q: Who is liable if the AI enters something wrong?
items.a: In the walkthrough the entry stands under the name of the person who connected the assistant. Your NIS 2 obligations do not change: management approves the measures and oversees their implementation. That is why a person should check every item before finishing it.

items.q: Who has to accept a risk assessment an AI produced?
items.a: Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2, management approves the measures. For certain digital services, point 2.1.1 of the Annex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 has management accept the results and residual risks, or an accountable person who reports to it. In the walkthrough an assistant rates in 2.3, but it cannot approve at 7.3.

items.q: Can we see later which entries came from AI?
items.a: Yes. Every screen an assistant wrote carries its name and the day. The activity log shows each change under the person's name, with “via” and the assistant's name.

items.q: Can a managing director leave the approval to their own assistant?
items.a: Not in the walkthrough. There is no tool for it, not for a managing director's assistant either. Management approves in the app, with its own account, and its name and the date then stand on each approved document.

meta.title: What can an MCP server fill in the NIS2 walkthrough?
meta.description: Item by item: what an AI assistant fills in the NIS2 walkthrough through the MCP server, under which rules, and what stays with you in the app.

whatItFills.title: What can an MCP server fill in the NIS2 walkthrough, and what not?
whatItFills.subtitle: In 19 of the 21 items an assistant fills in something through the MCP server: fields, lists, ratings, agreements, sign-ins, backups and the text of the policies. It writes only into items that are open or on the waiting list. Finishing, deciding, deleting suppliers, assets or trainings, and everything at 7.3 stay in the app.

sections.heading: Which items does the assistant fill in?
paragraphs: All but two. In 12.3 there is nothing to fill in: you read the item and finish it yourself. At 7.3 it fills in nothing, because a management review recorded there puts the item before management.
In the other 19 items it answers questions, fills lists, rates risks and writes policy drafts. The sections below show what exactly, item by item.

It has no tool for these steps: finishing an item, putting it on the waiting list, recording that the company decided not to do it, inviting a colleague. Only an assistant that can send a file itself, such as Claude Code, uploads a file as evidence.

sections.heading: Which rules hold for every item?
paragraphs: An assistant writes only into items that are open or on the waiting list. If it works on an item on the waiting list, it picks it up again, as the app does.
An item that is finished, decided against or signed is changed by a person in the app. If a signed item rests on a list, the server refuses any change to that list and names the items affected.
The server refuses an empty answer, so that no assistant erases what someone wrote. A field it leaves out stays as it is. It never deletes a supplier, an asset or a training.
If a person holds the Reviewer or Legal reviewer access role, their assistant only reads. Everyone else fills in items in the categories assigned to them, an admin in all of them.

sections.heading: Which questions and lists does it answer?
paragraphs: Fields are the single questions of an item. In 12.2 an assistant answers the account reference and the date of registration, in 3.3 whether you can sign in to the portal and report.

In 3.1 it records who leads in an emergency, the emergency number, how you reach each other when email and the network are down, and whom the person leading calls next. Then there are 11.2 (tools for phone, video and chat), 6.3 (address for vulnerability reports) and 12.4 (attack detection system, last evidence sent to the BSI).
It fills lists in 1.1 and 8.2, who was trained when, and in 5.1, your suppliers. It adds rows and corrects existing ones.
For a supplier linked through its own account, it cannot change the statements the supplier made itself.

sections.heading: What does it fill in for assets and risks?
paragraphs: In 2.2 it ticks on four lists what your company has, adds entries of its own and records who provides what. Our article on building an asset inventory with AI shows how in detail.

In 2.1 it can adopt the risk assessment method the walkthrough proposes. In 2.3 it rates software, technology and suppliers: how often something could happen and how badly it would hit, with a short note if wanted.
The risk map only shows the result.

sections.heading: What does it record for contracts, sign-ins and backups?
paragraphs: In 5.2 it records for each supplier whether the contract settles security and whether it provides for incident notification. In 11.1 it records for each sign-in whether it takes a second factor, and which one.
In 4.4 it notes for each backup system how often it backs up and on which day a restore last worked. In 4.2 it marks which processes must keep running without IT, with a line on how.
Each row is saved as it sends it. That is why the server tells it to read what is there first.

sections.heading: How does it write policies and the crypto list?
paragraphs: Six items write a document: 3.1, 2.4, 9.1, 10.1, 6.3 and 4.2. An assistant picks which sections of the template apply to your company and writes what else holds there.
What is saved is a draft, which management approves at 7.3. No assistant rewrites a document management has already approved, because a changed text loses the approval. That happens in the app.

In 9.1 it takes over the proposed list of accepted methods and can adapt it. When it changes the list, it sends the whole list: a method it leaves out is no longer on it. So read the list in the app before you finish 9.1.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Four items show how far an assistant goes and where you take over.
points: 2.2 Write down what your company has: the assistant ticks entries on the four lists and describes each one. You read each list, remove in the app what is wrong, and finish.
5.2 Record what you have agreed with your suppliers: it records for each supplier what the contract settles. What follows from that, you decide.
4.4 Record your backups: it records how often backups run and when a restore last worked. A date nobody knows is better left empty until someone has tried a restore.
11.1 Record where a second factor protects: it records for each sign-in whether a second factor applies. A sign-in without one ends up on the list management sees at 7.3 before approving.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 2.2, screen “Software for customers, staff and money”. At the top the mark “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”, below it the note that the entry “Warenwirtschaft (ERP)” is on your list.
walk.next: Create an account and start

items.q: Can the assistant finish an item once everything is filled in?
items.a: No, there is no tool for that. The server tells it what was saved and which fields are still empty, with the link to the item in the app. A person finishes it there.

items.q: What happens if I ask it to change a signed item?
items.a: The server refuses and tells the assistant that the change is made in the app, with the link to it. That way no assistant takes back a management signature.

items.q: Why does it not enter a management review at 7.3?
items.a: A review recorded there puts the item before management. That would finish it without the person working on it having decided so. That is why a person records the management review in the app.

items.q: Can it fill in items assigned to a colleague?
items.a: Only if you may work on that category yourself, because you are an admin or it is assigned to you. An assistant never has more rights than the person who connected it.

meta.title: MCP vs uploading documents to ChatGPT for NIS2 records
meta.description: Upload documents to ChatGPT, or connect an AI assistant over MCP? Who writes where, what gets checked and where the data goes, in the NIS2 walkthrough.

mcpVsChat.title: MCP or uploading documents to ChatGPT: what is the difference for NIS2?
mcpVsChat.subtitle: A chat such as ChatGPT gives you text that you paste somewhere yourself. An assistant connected over MCP writes straight into the NIS 2 walkthrough's lists, through the same checks as the app, under your name and marked on the screen. For a draft you read and paste in yourself, a chat is fine.

sections.heading: What is the difference between MCP and a chat with documents?
paragraphs: In a chat you upload an accounts payable list or an inventory and ask for a supplier list. Back comes text or a table, which you copy into your records by hand.

The chat knows only what you uploaded, as it stood on the day you uploaded it. What a colleague added to the walkthrough yesterday, it does not see. And later nobody can tell which row came from the chat.
An assistant connected over MCP reads the current state of your walkthrough before it writes: the answers so far and the rows already on a list. Then it enters each fact where it belongs.

sections.heading: What does the server check when the assistant enters data?
paragraphs: Every entry goes through the same checks as in the app; a date has to be a date, for example. Two more rules apply to assistants: the server refuses an empty answer, and it does not change a signed item.
What does not fit goes back to the assistant with the reason.
It saves as you, with your rights. The activity log shows the change under your name with “via” and the assistant's name. The screen shows which assistant wrote it on which day.

sections.heading: Where does the data go, in a chat and over MCP?
paragraphs: If the model runs at a vendor, that vendor sees what the assistant works with in both cases. In a chat that is what you upload or paste, over MCP it is what the assistant reads from the walkthrough.
Both run under your company's agreement with that vendor. If the assistant and the model run on your own hardware, nothing leaves your network.

Anthropic describes one difference for Claude. Feedback data, meaning what you send with the thumbs up or down button, does not include raw content from connectors, including remote and local MCP servers, “though data may be included if it's directly copied into your conversation with Claude”.

For its commercial products Anthropic also states that inputs and outputs are not used for training by default. We have not checked the terms of OpenAI or Microsoft; read your company's agreement with them.

sections.heading: When is a chat fine?
paragraphs: For a text you read and paste in yourself anyway. The security policy in 2.4, for example, has the field “Anything else that applies at your company (optional)”. You can have a chat draft that, read it, and copy it into the field.
Give the chat only what it needs for the wording, then. It does not need names, network diagrams or credentials for that.
For lists with many rows, and for facts someone should be able to trace later, a connected assistant has more going for it.

sections.heading: What does MCP not solve?
paragraphs: A connected assistant can be wrong just as a chat can. The mark on the screen shows you where to look, and you finish the item yourself.

Text in your records can also contain sentences a model takes for instructions. This is called prompt injection. In its baseline protection against indirect prompt injections (version 1.0, 14.09.2026) the BSI notes that no reliable countermeasure exists that removes the problem completely.
The server tells the assistant to treat everything it reads as data, and it marks filling in as a step that changes data. Choose an assistant that asks you before such a step.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: The difference shows in the lists at the start of the walkthrough and in the security policy.
points: 2.2 Write down what your company has: the assistant ticks the entries directly and describes them. You type nothing, but you do check.
Each of these changes then appears in the activity log under your name, with “via” and the assistant's name.
2.4 Write the security policy: both work here. An assistant picks the sections and writes what else applies, or you copy a draft from a chat into the field.
Either way the policy stays a draft until management approves it at 7.3.
walk.seeItAlt: The activity log, day by day: entries such as “Walkthrough item finished”, “Documents approved” and “Signed off by management”, each with the person's name and the time on the right.

items.q: Does the vendor see less of our data with MCP?
items.a: Not as such. What the assistant reads goes to its vendor, so the model can work with it. The difference lies in what you copy into a conversation yourself, and with Anthropic in what can end up in feedback data.

items.q: May a connected assistant do more than a chat?
items.a: Yes, it may write in your walkthrough, as you. That is why an admin first turns on “Allow AI assistants for this company”, and each person can disconnect theirs in Settings. A chat without a connection changes nothing in your records.

items.q: Can I use MCP directly in ChatGPT?
items.a: Yes, ChatGPT and Claude can add an MCP server as a custom connection and sign in through the browser for it. Articles of their own on ChatGPT and on Claude explain how. So far we have tested Claude Code, not these two.

items.q: Which is better for a first supplier list?
items.a: If your accounts payable list exists as a file, a connected assistant. It creates the suppliers in 5.1 directly in the list that 2.3 and 5.2 need later. You check the list and remove in the app anything that is not a supplier.

meta.title: Claude Code: add the NIS2 walkthrough as an MCP server
meta.description: Add an MCP server in Claude Code: one terminal command, one browser sign-in, and Claude Code reads and fills your NIS2 walkthrough. Plus a key for scripts.

claudeCode.title: How do I add the NIS2 walkthrough to Claude Code as an MCP server?
claudeCode.subtitle: The command claude mcp add puts the walkthrough into Claude Code as an MCP server. Then you type /mcp, sign in through the browser and allow access. From then on Claude Code reads your items in the NIS 2 walkthrough and fills in what they ask for; finishing and signing stay in the app.

sections.heading: How do I connect Claude Code with a browser sign-in?
paragraphs: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the protocol an AI assistant uses to talk to other software. Beforehand, an admin has turned on "Allow AI assistants for this company" in Settings, and your account has access to the walkthrough.
The command below adds the server to Claude Code, with the address https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp. Then start Claude Code, type /mcp and follow the steps in your browser.

After you sign in, the nisd2.eu page shows which assistant asks for which company and where the browser returns to. For Claude Code that is localhost with a port number: your own computer, where Claude Code receives the answer.
Click "Allow". If your last sign-in was more than 15 minutes ago, you sign in again first. The reason: an assistant stays connected even after you sign out of the browser.
sections.code: claude mcp add --transport http nisd2 https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp

sections.heading: How do I connect Claude Code with a key?
paragraphs: For scripts, or a computer without a browser, click "Create key" in Settings. The key is shown only at that moment. It lasts 90 days, in the company that was open when you made it.
Put it in the environment variable NISD2_MCP_KEY and add the server with the command below. The shell fills in the value when you run it, so your history holds only the variable's name.

Unless you say otherwise, Claude Code stores the server and its key in the file ~/.claude.json in your home folder. Do not use the project scope: it writes to .mcp.json in the project, a file Anthropic intends to be checked into the repository.
sections.code: claude mcp add --transport http nisd2 https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer $NISD2_MCP_KEY"

sections.heading: Does Claude Code reach an instance inside the company network?
paragraphs: Yes. Claude Code runs on your computer and connects from there, so it also reaches a self-hosted instance inside the company network. Put that instance's address in the commands instead of nisd2.eu.
Claude on the web and desktop, by contrast, connects from Anthropic's cloud, according to Anthropic. For that the instance has to be reachable from the internet.

sections.heading: What do I give Claude Code as a first task?
paragraphs: A file from your own records and an item. For 5.1 the list of creditors from your accounting fits, since almost everyone who works for you sends you invoices. An example request is below.
To fill an item in, Claude Code needs the item with its fields and the rows already on the list. The tool get_walkthrough returns both.

In "Manual" mode, according to Anthropic, Claude Code asks for permission the first time it uses each tool. Under /permissions the rule mcp__nisd2__get_walkthrough allows reading for good. Let filling in keep asking, so you confirm each change yourself.
We tested Claude Code on a local instance, with the browser sign-in and with a key. In the test on 14.10.2026 it read the walkthrough, filled in four items, left the rest open and signed nothing.
sections.code: Read item 5.1 of the NIS 2 walkthrough and add the suppliers from creditors.csv. Leave empty whatever the file does not show.

sections.heading: What stays with me afterwards?
paragraphs: Every screen Claude Code wrote carries a mark such as "Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026". The activity log shows each change under your name, "via" the assistant's name.
Finishing, deciding an item is not applicable and signing exist only in the app. No tool of an assistant can finish or sign an item.

The walkthrough is built on that. Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2 the management body, in a GmbH its managing directors, approves the measures and oversees their implementation. In Germany, § 38(1) BSIG obliges management to implement them and oversee their implementation.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Good first items are those whose answers already sit in your files.
points: 2.2 "Write down what your company has": from an inventory list or a licence overview, Claude Code ticks software and devices and enters on "Which software exactly, and from whom?" who provides them.
5.1 "Write down who works for you": the providers from 2.2 are already there. From the list of creditors, Claude Code adds the others, one line each with what they do for you.
4.4 "Record your backups": for each backup system on your list, Claude Code enters how often it backs up and when a restore from it last worked. If none has worked yet, the field stays empty.
Then you open each item in the app, check the marked screens and finish it.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect Claude Code

items.q: Can Claude Code upload files over MCP?
items.a: It is built for that, since Claude Code can send a file's bytes itself. The tool upload_file gives an address to upload to, then Claude Code attaches the file to the item, as evidence or as the certificate of a training. A file counts as evidence only once it is stored at its full size. We have not yet tested uploading with Claude Code itself.

items.q: Do I have to explain to Claude Code what NIS 2 requires?
items.a: No. For each item, get_walkthrough returns the walkthrough's own words, its fields with their schema and what is already entered. The server also gives every assistant instructions, such as entering only what your records show and leaving a field out when in doubt.

items.q: I belong to several companies. Which one does Claude Code work for?
items.a: The company that was open in the app when you allowed it or created the key. For another company, switch company in the app and connect again.

items.q: Does Claude Code stay connected when I sign out?
items.a: Yes. You disconnect in Settings under "Connected": one at a time with "Disconnect", or all at once with "Disconnect all assistants". Changing your password also disconnects every assistant.

items.q: How many MCP calls are allowed per hour?
items.a: 300 tool calls per person per hour, for all of that person's assistants together. Beyond that the server answers that there were too many calls in the last hour. The next hourly window starts fresh.

meta.title: Claude custom connector: connect the NIS2 walkthrough
meta.description: Add the NIS2 walkthrough to Claude on the web and desktop as a custom connector: which options to choose, and why the instance must be reachable online.

claude.title: How do I add the NIS2 walkthrough to Claude as a custom connector?
claude.subtitle: In Claude, add a custom connector with the address https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp, choose "Register automatically" and allow access. Claude connects from Anthropic's cloud, so the instance has to be reachable from the internet. We have not tested this route ourselves yet; the steps follow Anthropic's help pages.

sections.heading: How do I add a custom connector in Claude?
paragraphs: In Claude, a connector is the link to an MCP server. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the protocol an AI assistant uses to talk to other software. Beforehand, an admin has turned on "Allow AI assistants for this company" in the nisd2.eu Settings.
On Pro and Max, open "Customize", then "Connectors", then "+ Add" and "Add custom connector". Enter a name, for example nisd2, and the address below.
Under "Authentication", choose "Sign in now" or "Sign in when needed". Under "OAuth client", which asks how Claude identifies itself as a client, choose "Register automatically".

The recommended option "Use Claude's published identity" relies on a method the walkthrough's sign-in service does not offer. All labels are those in Anthropic's English help as of 16.10.2026; a German interface may name them differently.

sections.heading: Which Claude plan, and who adds the connector?
paragraphs: According to Anthropic, custom connectors are available on the Free, Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans; Free allows one.
On Team and Enterprise an Owner adds the connector for the organisation: "Organization settings", "Connectors", "Add", "Custom" and "Web", with the same details.
Everyone else then finds it under "Customize", "Connectors" and clicks "Connect". Each person signs in themselves.

sections.heading: What happens when I sign in?
paragraphs: Claude opens the nisd2.eu sign-in page. After you sign in, it shows which assistant asks for which company and where the browser returns to.
The assistant gives its name itself, so check the return address: it should belong to Anthropic. Click "Allow"; if your last sign-in was more than 15 minutes ago, you sign in again first.
Claude never sees your password in this. It gets a token, a kind of pass with an expiry date, which lasts an hour.
With a second token Claude renews it itself, until 90 days after your "Allow". Then you allow Claude again.

sections.heading: Why does the instance have to be reachable from the internet?
paragraphs: According to Anthropic, Claude connects to the server from Anthropic's cloud, not from your computer. That holds on the web and in the desktop app alike.
nisd2.eu is reachable from the internet over https. A self-hosted instance that runs only inside the company network cannot be reached by Claude this way.
For Enterprise, Anthropic describes tunnels into private networks, as a preview on request. Otherwise use Claude Code inside the company network, which runs on the computer.

sections.heading: What does Claude fill in the walkthrough?
paragraphs: Claude reads the items and fills in what they ask for, with your rights. It works best when you give it a list you already have in the chat and name the item.
A file as evidence needs an assistant that sends the file's bytes to storage itself. We have not tested whether Claude can do that from the chat, so upload evidence in the app.
Finishing and signing stay in the app too.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: In a chat, work item by item, with a list you already have.
points: 2.2 "Write down what your company has": with an inventory list in the chat, Claude ticks on the four lists what applies to you and enters who provides it.

3.1 "Plan what happens in an incident": on "Your emergency contacts", Claude enters who leads in an emergency, the IT emergency number, how you reach each other without email and network, and whom the person leading calls next.
From these answers the walkthrough writes your incident response plan. Claude can add below it what fits your company; read the plan in the app before you finish the item.
Every screen Claude wrote shows the assistant's name and the day.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect Claude

items.q: Can I use an API key in Claude instead of signing in?
items.a: Anthropic describes "Request headers" for API keys as a beta for a limited set of organisations. It recommends them for credentials a whole organisation shares, and the sign-in where each person uses their own account. The key from Settings belongs to one person, so use the browser sign-in for Claude.

items.q: Why does "Use Claude's published identity" not work?
items.a: With that option Claude identifies itself through a document Anthropic publishes on the internet (a Client ID Metadata Document). The walkthrough's sign-in service supports only automatic registration under RFC 7591. The MCP specification recommends the newer method and keeps automatic registration for servers that do not offer it.

items.q: Can Claude only read the walkthrough, without filling in?
items.a: Yes. According to Anthropic, under "Customize", "Connectors" you can set a single tool of the connector to "Blocked". Block fill_walkthrough_item, the tool that fills in, while Claude should only read.

items.q: What does Anthropic get to see of our data?
items.a: What Claude reads from the walkthrough goes to Anthropic, under your company's agreement with Anthropic. For commercial products such as Claude for Work, Anthropic states that it does not use inputs and outputs for training by default and acts as a processor there. Personal accounts come with their own terms; check those yourself.

items.q: Can Claude finish or sign an item?
items.a: No. No tool of an assistant finishes an item, decides one or signs. That stays in the app, and there only management can sign.

meta.title: Copilot Studio MCP: add the NIS2 walkthrough as a tool
meta.description: Set up Copilot Studio MCP: add the NIS2 walkthrough as a tool of an agent, with OAuth 2.0 and Dynamic discovery. What the agent may do after that.

copilotStudio.title: How do I connect Copilot Studio to the NIS2 walkthrough over MCP?
copilotStudio.subtitle: In Copilot Studio you add the walkthrough as a tool of an agent, with the address https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp and OAuth 2.0 with "Dynamic discovery" for sign-in. Copilot Studio runs in Microsoft's cloud, so as we understand it the instance has to be reachable from the internet over https. We have not tested this route yet.

sections.heading: How do I add the MCP server in Copilot Studio?
paragraphs: Copilot Studio is Microsoft's tool for an IT team to build its own agents, meaning assistants for particular tasks. Through MCP (Model Context Protocol), the protocol for such connections, the NIS 2 walkthrough becomes one of their tools.
Beforehand, an admin has turned on "Allow AI assistants for this company" in the nisd2.eu Settings. We have not tested Copilot Studio yet; the steps follow Microsoft's guide as of 15.10.2026.

In the agent, open the Tools page, then "Add a tool", "New tool" and "Model Context Protocol". The MCP onboarding wizard opens. According to Microsoft, Copilot Studio supports Streamable HTTP, and has not supported the older SSE since August 2025; the walkthrough answers over Streamable HTTP.

Fill in Server name, Server description and Server URL, with the address below. The agent reads the description to decide when to call the server, for example: Reads and fills in the company's NIS 2 walkthrough.

sections.heading: Which authentication do I choose?
paragraphs: OAuth is the usual way for software to sign in on your behalf without knowing your password. Choose OAuth 2.0 as the authentication type and "Dynamic discovery" as its type.
Copilot Studio then finds the sign-in addresses itself and registers with the sign-in service that every instance runs itself.

Select "Create", then "Next". On "Add tool", create a connection with "Create a new connection" and add the server with "Add to agent". Connecting opens the nisd2.eu sign-in page: sign in, check the return address, "Allow".

According to Microsoft, with OAuth 2.0 the individual users of the agent sign in themselves and grant it permission. In the walkthrough the agent then works with the rights of the person who signed in.

sections.heading: Does an API key work too?
paragraphs: Copilot Studio also offers an API key, in a header or as a query in the address. The walkthrough expects the key in the Authorization header, as "Bearer", a space, then the key.
It does not accept the key in the address. We have not checked whether Copilot Studio sends the header in that form, so use OAuth 2.0.

sections.heading: Does the instance have to be reachable from the internet?
paragraphs: Copilot Studio is a service in Microsoft's cloud. So we assume that Microsoft opens the connection and that the instance has to be reachable from the internet over https. Microsoft's guide does not say so explicitly.

nisd2.eu is reachable that way. A self-hosted instance only inside the company network would then not be reachable along this route; we have not checked whether Microsoft offers a way in. Inside the company network, software that runs on the computer works, such as Claude Code.

In Copilot Studio, access to MCP servers runs through the Power Platform: according to Microsoft, a data policy for connectors also governs the MCP server and its tools. Ask whoever manages the Power Platform at your company whether a policy allows the server.

sections.heading: What may the agent do in the walkthrough?
paragraphs: The agent reads the items and fills in fields, lists and screens, with the signed-in person's rights.
It cannot finish an item, decide it is not applicable, delete a supplier, an asset or a training, or sign. The server offers those functions to no assistant.
What the agent reads goes to Microsoft, under your company's agreement with Microsoft. We did not check Microsoft's terms on this for this article.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: For an IT team that works in Microsoft 365, two items suggest themselves.
points: 5.1 "Write down who works for you": the agent adds to your list of suppliers, one line each with what they do for you. The item counts everyone who can reach your data, so Microsoft as the agent's vendor belongs there too.

10.1 "Write the staff, access and asset policy": the template has fixed sections on joining, changing role and leaving, on outside staff, on access and on managing your IT. The agent picks the clauses that fit and adds below what applies to you, for example how Microsoft 365 accounts are blocked on the last working day.
Every screen the agent wrote shows its name and the day. The person reads the policy in the app and finishes the item there; management approves it, in the app as well.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect Copilot Studio

items.q: What rights does the Copilot Studio agent get?
items.a: Those of the person who signs in: their areas of the walkthrough, or all of them for an admin. The agent of someone who only reviews the walkthrough can read it but fills in nothing. If an admin lets assistants read the records and the person may export, the agent also reads all of the company's records.

items.q: How long does the agent stay connected?
items.a: With the refresh token the walkthrough hands out, Copilot Studio can renew the sign-in itself. It ends at the latest 90 days after "Allow", and then the person signs in again. A new password ends it sooner.

items.q: How do I disconnect Copilot Studio again?
items.a: In the nisd2.eu Settings under "Connected" with "Disconnect", or all at once with "Disconnect all assistants". For the whole company, an admin turns "Allow AI assistants for this company" off. The connection ends at its next call.

items.q: Is there a limit on MCP calls?
items.a: Yes, 300 tool calls per person per hour, for all of that person's assistants together. The next hourly window starts fresh.

items.q: Can I see in the walkthrough what the agent entered?
items.a: Yes. Every screen it wrote carries its name and the day. The activity log shows each change under the person's name, "via" the agent's name.

meta.title: Connect VS Code, Cursor and Gemini CLI to NIS2 over MCP
meta.description: Connect VS Code, Cursor and Gemini CLI to the NIS2 walkthrough over MCP: what a client needs, where the key belongs and how to judge an assistant.

otherAssistants.title: How do I connect VS Code, Cursor or Gemini CLI to the NIS2 walkthrough over MCP?
otherAssistants.subtitle: Any client that talks to an MCP server over Streamable HTTP and either signs in through the browser with automatic registration or sends a key in a header can read and fill in the walkthrough. The steps for VS Code, Cursor and Gemini CLI follow the vendors' guides as of 16.10.2026. We have tested none of them ourselves.

sections.heading: What does a client need for the MCP server?
paragraphs: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the protocol an AI assistant uses to talk to other software. The client has to reach the MCP server over the network, using Streamable HTTP, at https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp or your own instance's address.

It can sign in two ways. Through the browser under OAuth 2.1 with automatic registration (Dynamic Client Registration), or with a key from Settings, which it sends in the Authorization header as Bearer.
The walkthrough's sign-in service offers no other way, such as published client documents (Client ID Metadata Documents) or fixed client credentials. So far we have tested Claude Code.
According to OpenAI, ChatGPT cannot present custom API keys, so only the browser sign-in can work there. Our own article on ChatGPT explains the setup.

sections.heading: How do I connect VS Code with GitHub Copilot?
paragraphs: In VS Code you add the server to the file mcp.json, with the type http and the address. Microsoft advises against hardcoding API keys there and points to input variables or environment files instead.
VS Code runs on your computer, so it also reaches an instance inside the company network. For some servers it shows a dialog on first start, where you decide whether to trust it.

sections.heading: How do I connect Cursor?
paragraphs: Cursor speaks Streamable HTTP. For OAuth sign-in, its guide names fixed client credentials as the exception for servers without automatic registration.
The walkthrough offers automatic registration, so the browser sign-in should work. We have not tested it.

Alternatively Cursor sends headers from its mcp.json, so it can send the key too, reading the value from an environment variable. According to Cursor, it asks for approval by default before using an MCP server's tools.

sections.heading: How do I connect Gemini CLI?
paragraphs: Gemini CLI signs in through the browser as soon as the server asks for it. With /mcp auth nisd2 you start the sign-in yourself.

With a key, add the server as below. The option -s user stores it in your user settings (~/.gemini/settings.json); without it, according to Google, it lands in .gemini/settings.json in the project, key included.
Do not set trust to true for this server. According to Google, that makes Gemini CLI skip every confirmation before a tool call, including before filling in.
sections.code: gemini mcp add -s user --transport http --header "Authorization: Bearer $NISD2_MCP_KEY" nisd2 https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp

sections.heading: How do I judge an assistant?
paragraphs: Does it ask before it changes data? The tool that fills in is marked as one that changes data, and a client that asks before such calls asks here. The MCP specification recommends that a person can deny any tool call.

Does it run on your computer or in the vendor's cloud? VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Claude Code run on the computer and also reach an instance inside the company network. According to their vendors, ChatGPT and Claude on the web need an instance reachable from the internet, or a tunnel; for Copilot Studio we assume the same.

Where does the data go? What the assistant reads goes to the vendor of its model, even when the program runs on your computer, under your company's agreement with that vendor. If both the program and the model run on your own hardware, the walkthrough data stays in your network.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Whichever assistant you use, item 2.2 is a good first task.
points: 2.2 "Write down what your company has" has four lists to tick: what your company does every day, software for customers, staff and money, software everyone uses, and technology and rooms.
Then the item asks which software and which technology exactly, and from whom. A provider the assistant names there then appears on your supplier list in 5.1.
Give the assistant an inventory list and ask it to leave open whatever the list does not show. The server gives every assistant the same instruction.
Every screen an assistant wrote shows its name and the day. You finish the item in the app.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect an assistant

items.q: Are there European AI assistants with MCP?
items.a: Mistral Le Chat and Langdock describe their own connections to MCP servers in their documentation. We have checked neither the details nor a connection to the walkthrough. Judge whether they fit with the questions above.

items.q: My client cannot find the sign-in. What now?
items.a: Without a key the server answers 401 and points to its description at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/api/mcp. From there a client finds the sign-in service and the automatic registration. If your client cannot do that, use the key.

items.q: How do we connect our own script or agent?
items.a: With the key: it lasts 90 days, in one company, and is sent in the Authorization header as Bearer. The tools get_walkthrough, fill_walkthrough_item and upload_file describe their own inputs as JSON Schema.

items.q: Can an assistant delete anything over MCP?
items.a: No tool deletes a supplier, an asset or a training, finishes an item or signs. It can replace, though: an answer with a new one, a row with a corrected one, and in 9.1 the crypto list as a whole, where a method it leaves out drops off the list. It cannot empty a field; a person removes a wrong row in the app.

meta.title: MCP OAuth or API key: which to use and how long each lasts
meta.description: MCP OAuth or API key for the NIS2 walkthrough: when to sign in through the browser, when to use the key, how long each lasts and what ends it.

keyOrSignIn.title: Should I connect MCP with OAuth or with an API key?
keyOrSignIn.subtitle: Use OAuth, the sign-in through the browser, wherever your assistant supports it: you copy no secret, and access renews itself until 90 days after your "Allow". Use the API key, called "key" in the app, for scripts and software without a browser. It lasts 90 days and is shown only once.

sections.heading: When do I use OAuth, and when the API key?
paragraphs: OAuth, wherever the client supports it. Claude Code, Claude on the web and desktop, Copilot Studio and ChatGPT describe the browser sign-in in their guides; according to OpenAI, ChatGPT cannot send a key.
So far we have tested Claude Code, both ways.
The API key for scripts, your own agents and software that cannot open a browser. Keep it in an environment variable or a password manager, in no file you share or put in a repository.

sections.heading: How does the OAuth sign-in work?
paragraphs: The assistant opens your instance's sign-in page. You sign in, see which assistant asks for which company and where the browser returns to, and click "Allow".
OAuth is the way for software to sign in on your behalf without seeing your password. The walkthrough uses OAuth 2.1 with PKCE: only the client that started the sign-in can collect the access.
The client registers itself along the way (Dynamic Client Registration). The instance is its own sign-in service, so even when self-hosted no third party is involved.

sections.heading: How long does the OAuth sign-in last?
paragraphs: The assistant gets two tokens, passes with an expiry date. It calls the walkthrough with the access token, which lasts an hour. With the refresh token it gets a new one, and every renewal also replaces the refresh token, which lasts 30 days.
If the same refresh token comes in again within a minute, the server still accepts it. That happens when a client renews twice at once, or an answer is lost on the way.

If it comes in again later, the server treats it as copied and disconnects every assistant of that person, the key included. If the original and a copy both renewed within that minute, it shows once both renew again.
At the latest 90 days after your "Allow", the sign-in ends, however often the assistant renewed. Then you allow it again.

sections.heading: How does the API key work?
paragraphs: In Settings, "Create key" makes a key. It is shown only at that moment and stored nowhere, so the app cannot show it again.
It lasts 90 days, as you and with your role, in the company that was open when you made it. The client sends it in the Authorization header as Bearer.
You hold one key per company. A new one ends the previous key; assistants that signed in through the browser stay connected.

sections.heading: Why do both ask for a recent sign-in?
paragraphs: Both survive signing out of the browser: an assistant stays connected even after you sign out. That is why "Create key" and "Allow" ask for a sign-in from the last 15 minutes.
With an older session the page sends you to sign in and then brings you back.
The app tells you by email about every new connection. If it was not you, disconnect all assistants and change your password.

sections.heading: What ends a connection?
paragraphs: "Disconnect" in Settings ends one connection at its next call. "Disconnect all assistants" and any change to your password end the key and every browser sign-in at once.

If you leave the company or are removed, both end for good. If an admin turns off "Allow AI assistants for this company", every member's connections end. Our article on revoking MCP access has the details.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: How people sign in is itself an item of the walkthrough.
points: 11.1 "Record where a second factor protects": for each program and access on your list, the item records how people sign in: password only, with a second factor and which one, or not known yet.

A connected assistant can fill this in. Each row starts at "Password only", the safe assumption; give it a source, such as an overview from your account administration, and have it choose "Not known yet" where the source shows nothing.
List the assistant itself in 2.2 under "Software everyone uses", and 11.1 then also asks how you sign in to it.
Every screen an assistant wrote shows its name and the day; you finish 11.1 in the app.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect an assistant

items.q: Does the MCP server support Dynamic Client Registration or CIMD?
items.a: Only Dynamic Client Registration under RFC 7591: the client registers itself at its first sign-in. Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD), a published document a client identifies itself with, are not supported by the sign-in service. That is why you choose "Register automatically" in Claude.

items.q: Can I connect several assistants at once?
items.a: Yes. Each browser sign-in is a connection of its own, plus one key per company. Settings lists them all under "Connected", with the day each was connected and last used, and each can be disconnected on its own.

items.q: What happens after 90 days?
items.a: The key stops working; create a new one and enter it in the client. A browser sign-in ends 90 days after "Allow", and then you allow the assistant again.

items.q: Does an API key work for several companies?
items.a: No. It works in the company that was open when you made it. For another company, switch in the app and create a key there.

meta.title: Build an asset inventory with AI: NIS2 walkthrough item 2.2
meta.description: Build an asset inventory with AI: an AI assistant fills item 2.2 of the NIS2 walkthrough from your inventory list. What it enters, and what you check.

assets.title: How do I build an asset inventory for NIS2 with AI?
assets.subtitle: An AI assistant connected over MCP fills the lists in item 2.2 of the NIS 2 walkthrough from your own records: it ticks entries in the catalogue, adds your own and says who provides what. Every screen it wrote shows its name and the day. You check the list and finish the item in the app.

sections.heading: How does an AI assistant build the inventory?
paragraphs: An asset inventory is the list of what your company needs for its work: processes, software, technology and rooms. In the NIS 2 walkthrough you keep it in item 2.2, and a connected AI assistant can fill it there from your records.

It connects through MCP (Model Context Protocol), an open standard that lets an assistant such as Claude read and enter data in an application. It then works with the rights of the person who connected it.

Give it what you already have: your IT provider's inventory, a licence list, or an export from your CMDB, the database where your IT keeps its devices and software. The assistant matches the lines to catalogue entries, ticks those and adds entries of its own for the rest.
The server tells every assistant to enter only what your records and systems show, and to leave a field empty rather than guess. Whether it did, you can see on the list itself.

sections.heading: What belongs in the asset inventory under NIS 2?
sections.law: Art. 21(2)(a) and (i) NIS 2 · § 30(2) no. 1 and 9 BSIG
paragraphs: Item 2.2 keeps four lists: “What your company does every day” (your processes), “Software for customers, staff and money”, “Software everyone uses” and “Technology and rooms”. Each comes with a catalogue to tick, 132 entries in all, such as “Accounting software (DATEV, Lexware, sevDesk, lexoffice)” or “Laptops and desktops”.

Then come “Which software exactly, and from whom?” and “Which technology exactly, and from whom?”. For each entry they record what you actually use, what for, whether it runs in house or in the cloud, and who provides it.

The directive counts policies on risk analysis and asset management among the minimum measures. In Germany, the BSIG asks for concepts for managing your ICT systems, products and processes; a list is the usual first step.

A complete, up to date inventory is required in so many words by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690, Annex point 12.4. It applies directly only to certain digital services, such as cloud and data centre providers.

sections.heading: What does the AI not do with the inventory?
paragraphs: It does not finish item 2.2, and it takes nothing off the list: none of its tools deletes an entry from this list. If something wrong is on it, you take it off in the app.
It works on items that are still open or that you set aside. Once you have finished 2.2, the server takes nothing more from the assistant on that item; you make changes in the app.
While an item that relies on this list is signed off, such as 2.2 itself or 4.4 on backups, the tools refuse any change to the list. They name the items concerned.
The change would take that sign-off back. That is a person's step in the app, and the item then goes to management again.

sections.heading: How do I check what the AI entered?
paragraphs: Every screen an assistant wrote carries a mark at the top, for example “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”. The assistant gives that name itself. The mark stays even if you change the screen afterwards.

The activity log lists every change under the name of the person who connected the assistant, with “via” and the assistant's name. That keeps changes made in the browser apart from changes made through the assistant.

Before you finish, go through all four lists and both detail screens. Look out for software you rent from the cloud, such as email or accounting: the walkthrough names it as often missed, and a plain device list will not contain it.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Item 2.2 turns into work on six screens, and item 2.3 builds directly on it.
points: 2.2, the four lists from “What your company does every day” to “Technology and rooms”: the assistant ticks catalogue entries and adds entries of its own from your records.

2.2, “Which software exactly, and from whom?” and “Which technology exactly, and from whom?”: it records what exactly each thing is, where it runs and who provides it. Those providers then appear on your supplier list in 5.1.
You go through every screen that carries the assistant's mark, take off what is wrong, add what is missing and finish 2.2 in the app.
2.3 “Rate your risks”: every piece of software and technology on the list gets a level from frequency and damage. Management signs off at the end, in 7.3.
walk.seeItAlt: Item 2.2 of the NIS 2 walkthrough, screen “Software for customers, staff and money”, with the assistant's mark at the top naming claude-code/2.1.287 and 16 October 2026, and the entry “Warenwirtschaft (ERP)” on the list
walk.next: Start your list in the walkthrough

items.q: Do I have to go through the whole catalogue myself?
items.a: No. You check what is on the list, add what is missing and take off what is wrong in the app. The walkthrough itself says the list does not have to be perfect: when something new comes along, you add it later.

items.q: Which records help the AI most?
items.a: What your company already keeps: your IT provider's inventory, a licence list, a CMDB export. For the providers, the list of creditors helps, because the provider is whoever sends you the invoice. Claude Code runs on your computer and can read such files there; an assistant in the browser gets the file however it accepts files, for example as an attachment in the chat.

items.q: What happens to the providers the AI names?
items.a: Every provider name not yet on your supplier list is added there as a new supplier, and is then already in 5.1. If the assistant leaves a provider out for a program, the two are no longer linked, and the provider stays on the supplier list. One call may name at most 50 different providers; for more, the assistant makes several calls.

items.q: Does the AI assistant itself belong in the asset inventory?
items.a: We recommend it, if you use one. Add it on “Software everyone uses” and its vendor on “Which software exactly, and from whom?”. The vendor then also appears on your supplier list in 5.1.

items.q: Does the vendor of my assistant see our inventory?
items.a: What the assistant reads goes to its vendor, under your company's agreement with that vendor. Which assistant you use is your choice. With an assistant and a model running on your own hardware, nothing leaves your network.

meta.title: NIS2 supplier register with AI: build it, check contracts
meta.description: An AI assistant builds your NIS2 supplier register from your list of creditors and records what each contract settles: walkthrough items 5.1 and 5.2.

suppliers.title: How do I build a NIS2 supplier register with AI?
suppliers.subtitle: Give a connected AI assistant your list of creditors and your contracts. It adds one line per supplier in item 5.1 and ticks in 5.2 what the contracts settle on security and incidents. It cannot finish an item: you check every line, and management signs off at the end.

sections.heading: How does an AI assistant build the supplier register?
paragraphs: An AI assistant connects to your company in the app through MCP (Model Context Protocol), an open standard. It fills in the NIS 2 walkthrough as the person who connected it.

Almost everyone who works for you sends you invoices. That is why item 5.1 starts from the list of creditors in your accounting, covering the last twelve months, for example from DATEV. Give the assistant that list and your contracts and subscriptions.
It adds one line per supplier, with the name and what the supplier does for you. Tell it what the walkthrough recommends: when in doubt, write it down rather than leave it out.
Whoever you named in item 2.2 as the provider of your software and technology is already on the list. The assistant sees the existing lines, with an instruction not to add them again.

sections.heading: Who belongs on the supplier register under NIS 2?
paragraphs: Item 5.1, “Write down who works for you”, is a list of your direct suppliers and service providers. It covers everyone who touches your IT or your data, including the tax adviser with access to staff data.

The directive requires supply chain security, including the security-related aspects of your relationships with your direct suppliers. You take into account the vulnerabilities specific to each supplier (Art. 21(3) NIS 2).

For certain digital services, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 names a registry of direct suppliers with contact points (Annex point 5.2). Whether your AI assistant's own vendor belongs on this list is covered in our article on the AI vendor as a supplier.

sections.heading: What does the assistant record about contracts in 5.2?
paragraphs: Item 5.2, “Record what you have agreed with your suppliers”, asks two things per supplier. Do the contract, the data processing agreement or the terms set security requirements, for example on access and updates? And does the supplier have to report security incidents to you?

The assistant reads the contracts, data processing agreements or standard terms you give it and sets the two ticks per supplier. Large providers rarely negotiate; then what counts is their standard terms. If neither is settled, “None of this is agreed” is the right answer.
Next to each name, 5.2 shows the level from item 2.3, where each supplier is rated by frequency and damage. So you can see where an agreement matters most.
For its digital services, the Implementing Regulation names points that contracts should specify where appropriate, among them security requirements and incident notification (Annex point 5.1.4).

sections.heading: What goes into a line, and what may the assistant change?
paragraphs: On the screen “Your suppliers” in 5.1 there are two fields: “Supplier” and “What they do for you”. The supplier list holds more, such as a contact person and email, whether the supplier has access to your systems or data, and when the contract starts and ends.
A new line needs only the name. The assistant can correct a line that is already there; fields it does not send stay as they are.
It cannot delete a line. You do that in the app.

sections.heading: What happens to statements a supplier made itself?
paragraphs: If a supplier has accepted your invitation to the security questionnaire, its line is linked to its own company in the supplier portal. What it stated there, for example whether it offers a data processing agreement or helps with incidents, are its own statements.
The assistant receives them set apart, under writtenBySupplier, and cannot change them. The server refuses and says these are the supplier's own statements from its portal.

A text written by others can try to slip instructions to the assistant (prompt injection). The server therefore tells the assistant to read everything as data, never as instructions. It says so in its instructions and in the description of the tool that reads the walkthrough.

Germany's BSI writes that no reliable countermeasure exists that removes the problem completely. What the server itself enforces holds regardless: no tool finishes an item, deletes a line or signs anything.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Suppliers turn into work at two items of the walkthrough, and the rating between them connects the two.
points: 5.1 “Write down who works for you”, screen “Your suppliers”: the assistant adds one line per supplier from the list of creditors. Whoever 2.2 names as a provider is already there.
2.3, “Rate your suppliers”: each supplier gets a level from frequency and damage, which then also shows on the supplier list.
5.2, “What each one has agreed”: the assistant sets the ticks for security requirements and incident reporting per supplier. You check every line and finish 5.1 and 5.2 in the app.

7.3: a supplier rated high or very high whose contract settles neither security nor incidents appears as an open point by itself before the sign-off. You set in the app who takes care of it and by when.
walk.seeItAlt: The start page of the NIS 2 walkthrough, with “Your path” on the right listing the items in order, the first three ticked, and “Write down who works for you” further down
walk.next: Build your supplier list

items.q: How does the assistant know who counts as a supplier?
items.a: From the records you give it and from the walkthrough's own words, which it reads along. They say who is meant: every direct supplier and service provider that touches your IT or your data. Whether the list is right, you decide when you check it, before you finish 5.1.

items.q: What if nothing is agreed with a supplier?
items.a: Then “None of this is agreed” is the right answer. The walkthrough suggests raising it, for example at the next renewal. You can send the supplier the security questionnaire from its line, or your assistant does.

items.q: Can the assistant change the supplier list after the sign-off?
items.a: No. Once 5.1 is signed off, the server refuses every new line and every correction from the assistant, because it would take the sign-off back. The same holds for the detail screens in 2.2, the ratings in 2.3 and the ticks in 5.2, which can change the supplier list. The refusal names the items concerned; you change it in the app, and the item then goes to management again.

items.q: How many suppliers does the assistant add at once?
items.a: Up to 50 new lines per call, and in 5.2 up to 500 suppliers at once. Each person may make 300 calls an hour. A long list of creditors therefore takes several calls.

items.q: Does my suppliers' data end up with the AI assistant's vendor?
items.a: What the assistant reads goes to its vendor, under your company's agreement with that vendor. For Anthropic's commercial products, Anthropic acts as a processor, and inputs are not used for training by default. We have not checked the terms of other vendors.
