meta.title: NIS2 and the AI Act: what applies when AI helps
meta.description: NIS 2 governs your company's cybersecurity, the AI Act governs AI systems. What both ask when an AI assistant helps with the NIS 2 walkthrough.

aiActNis2.title: NIS2 and the AI Act: what applies when an AI assistant helps?
aiActNis2.subtitle: If a company under NIS 2 uses an AI assistant, both laws apply, to different questions. NIS 2 requires you to protect your IT and management to approve the measures. Under the AI Act your company is a “deployer” and takes measures to support its staff's AI literacy. On our reading, filling in NIS 2 records triggers no high-risk duties.

sections.heading: What does NIS 2 govern, and what does the AI Act govern?
paragraphs: NIS 2, Directive (EU) 2022/2555, requires essential and important entities to take measures that protect their network and information systems (Art. 21). Management approves these measures and oversees their implementation (Art. 20(1)).

The AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, governs AI systems according to their risk. It applies, among others, to providers placing AI systems on the market in the EU and to deployers established in the EU (Art. 2(1)). Whether your company falls under NIS 2 plays no part in this.
The two do not refer to each other. The AI Act does not mention NIS 2, and NIS 2 mentions AI only in recitals 51 and 89, as encouragement to use it for cybersecurity.

sections.heading: Is your company a deployer under the AI Act?
paragraphs: Yes, if it uses an AI assistant at work. Under Art. 3(4) AI Act a deployer is anyone using an AI system under its authority, except in the course of a personal non-professional activity. The provider is whoever develops the system and places it on the market under its own name (Art. 3(3)), as a rule the maker of your assistant.
Mind the German wording: the German text calls a deployer “Betreiber”, the same word the BSIG uses for operators of critical facilities. In the AI Act it means anyone using an AI system at work.

Art. 50 sets out transparency duties. Those of deployers concern emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, deep fakes and text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. On our reading, internal NIS 2 records are none of these.

sections.heading: Is an AI assistant that fills in NIS 2 records a high-risk system?
paragraphs: High-risk systems include those listed in Annex III (Art. 6(2)). Point 2 covers critical infrastructure: AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity.

Since the amendment by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Art. 6(1a) says it outright: AI systems used solely for non-safety related aspects of user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation or convenience or quality control do not qualify as safety components. Recital 55 already states that components intended solely for cybersecurity purposes should not qualify as safety components.

Our reading, not an authority's: an assistant that fills in lists and texts in the walkthrough assists users and takes writing off their hands. If it gets something wrong, a wrong entry sits in your records, which a person can correct. So the counter-rule in Art. 6(1b) for systems whose failure or malfunctioning would endanger health and safety does not apply, and neither does Annex III point 2. An AI system that controls a facility is a separate question.

Even a system listed in Annex III is not high-risk under Art. 6(3) where it poses no significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, for example because it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task or a preparatory task to an assessment. A provider who classifies its system this way documents its assessment (Art. 6(4)).
sections.law: Annex III point 2 · Art. 6(1a), 6(1b), 6(3) and 6(4) AI Act · recital 55

sections.heading: What does the AI Act ask of you as a deployer?
paragraphs: Art. 4 AI Act, since 27 July 2026 in the version of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744: providers and deployers take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and of other persons dealing with AI systems on their behalf. They do not have to guarantee any specific level for anyone. The Commission and the Member States support SMEs in particular (Art. 4(2)).
Our suggestion for a start in the walkthrough: whoever connects an assistant knows what it may fill in there, that it can be wrong, and how to recognise its entries.

The duties for high-risk systems apply from 2 December 2027 for systems under Annex III and from 2 August 2028 for systems under Annex I (Art. 113, also amended). They include the deployer duties in Art. 26, such as human oversight.
sections.law: Art. 4, Art. 26 and Art. 113 AI Act, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744

sections.heading: Where do NIS 2 and the AI Act meet in your company?
paragraphs: For NIS 2 the assistant is software your company uses (2.2) and its vendor a supplier (5.1). Our article on the AI vendor as a supplier shows what that means in detail.

Two training duties sit close together. Art. 20(2) NIS 2 requires the members of management to follow cybersecurity training; in Germany this is § 38(3) BSIG. Art. 4 AI Act concerns the AI literacy of everyone working with AI systems. The walkthrough asks about the first one in 1.1.

Management approves the measures (Art. 20(1) NIS 2); in Germany, § 38(1) BSIG obliges it to implement them and oversee their implementation. In the walkthrough no assistant has a tool for the approval.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: At its start and its end the walkthrough shows what stays with management; it does not cover the AI Act itself.
points: 1.1 “Get management trained”, screen “One line per person”: this holds the last training of each member of management. An assistant can enter the rows; management has to attend itself.
2.2 and 5.1: the assistant is on your software list, its vendor on the supplier list.
7.3 “Record the management review”: before the approval the walkthrough shows open points, for example “No management training in the last three years.” You set who takes care of each and by when.

On the screen “Management approves the documents” management reads each document and approves it, signed in with its own account. It then reads “Approved on” with the date and the name. An assistant fills in nothing in 7.3.
walk.seeItAlt: An item of the NIS 2 walkthrough approved by management: marked “Approved”, with the date and the name of the member of management
walk.next: Prepare training and approval

items.q: Does the AI Act apply to companies that fall under NIS 2?
items.a: Yes, once they are established in the EU and use AI systems at work, because that makes them deployers (Art. 2(1)(b) and Art. 3(4) AI Act). This holds whether or not a company falls under NIS 2.

items.q: Do we have to declare AI systems in the NIS 2 registration?
items.a: The details Art. 3(4) NIS 2 lists for registration do not include AI systems: the entity's name, address and contact details including IP ranges, the sector and the Member States where it provides services. In Germany, § 33(1) BSIG adds the legal form, the commercial register number and the competent supervisory authorities, and no AI systems either. In the walkthrough, registration is item 12.2.

items.q: Do we need an AI officer?
items.a: The AI Act requires none from deployers; no such role appears in its text. Art. 4 asks for measures on AI literacy, and you decide who in the company drives them. For cybersecurity, NIS 2 places the responsibility with management.

items.q: Does the AI Act require a human to check what the AI enters?
items.a: The deployer's duty of human oversight sits in Art. 26(2) and applies to high-risk systems, for Annex III systems from 2 December 2027. For your NIS 2 records, NIS 2 is what counts: management approves the measures and oversees their implementation. In the walkthrough a person finishes every item, and management signs off in 7.3.

meta.title: AI-generated NIS2 documentation in an audit: what counts
meta.description: No authority has said whether NIS 2 records filled in by AI pass an audit. What supervisors can ask for, and what the NIS 2 walkthrough shows them.

auditAiDocs.title: Do NIS2 records filled in by AI hold up in an audit?
auditAiDocs.subtitle: No authority has ruled on this so far, as far as we could check (as of October 2026). NIS 2 does not ask who typed a text. Supervisors can ask for evidence that your measures are implemented. So what they can check is whether your records describe what your company does, and whether management approved the measures.

sections.heading: Has any authority allowed or rejected NIS 2 records written by AI?
paragraphs: No, as far as we could check (as of October 2026). We found no statement from the BSI, ENISA or national authorities on whether records written by AI count.

The legal texts do not settle it either. NIS 2 mentions AI only in two recitals, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 not at all. What they require is measures (Art. 21 NIS 2) and their approval by management (Art. 20(1)).

The German BSIG expressly requires companies to document how they comply with their duty to take risk management measures (§ 30(1) sentence 3 BSIG). None of these provisions says who has to type the document.
sections.law: Art. 20(1) and Art. 21 NIS 2 · § 30(1) sentence 3 BSIG

sections.heading: What can supervisors ask for in an audit?
paragraphs: For essential entities, the authority may, among other things, carry out on-site inspections and regular and targeted security audits by an independent body or by the authority itself. It can request information, including your documented policies, and evidence of their implementation (Art. 32(2) NIS 2).

For important entities, the authority acts after the fact, when it has evidence, indications or information that an entity allegedly does not comply with NIS 2 (Art. 33(1)). It then has similar means, without regular audits.

In Germany, § 61 BSIG covers particularly important entities and § 62 BSIG important ones. In a review, a particularly important entity hands over the relevant records, documents and other papers on request (§ 61(5)). For an important entity, the BSI can take the same measures where facts suggest it does not implement its duties, or not correctly (§ 62). Operators of critical facilities prove implementation every three years through security audits, examinations or certifications (§ 39 BSIG).

sections.heading: What matters for records an AI filled in?
paragraphs: That they are true. Supervisors can ask for evidence that your policies are implemented (Art. 32(2)(g) and Art. 33(2)(f) NIS 2). A policy describing measures your company does not have does not help with that.

ComplianceForge, a seller of documentation templates and so not neutral, writes from practice: “Auditors don't just review documentation, they compare it to reality.” In other words, auditors hold the records up against what actually happens in the company.

A language model can invent details that sound plausible: a backup schedule that never existed, or a second factor that is not switched on. So the walkthrough's server instructs the assistant to enter only what your documents and systems show, and to leave a field empty rather than guess. That instruction does not guarantee the model follows it.

sections.heading: What does the walkthrough show an auditor?
paragraphs: Every change appears in the activity log under the name of the person who made it. If it came through an assistant, it reads “via” and the assistant's name. Every screen an assistant wrote also carries a mark, for example “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”.

Only a person can finish an item; no assistant can. In 7.3 management approves the documents, signed in with its own account. Each document then reads “Approved on” with the date and the name. For each open point, the screen records who takes care of it and by when.

The export “Everything in one document” sums up the whole walkthrough: status, open points, documents, risk matrix and all registers, each requirement with its approval. Admins, reviewers and management can export. The export does not show which entries came from an assistant; the mark in the app and the activity log show that.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Before an audit, four places in the walkthrough matter.
points: Screens with an assistant's mark: read these first, and check especially what only someone in the company can know, for example when a backup was last restored (4.4).
The activity log in the left sidebar under Administration: admins and people with the reviewer or legal reviewer role see which changes came through an assistant and who changed anything afterwards.
7.3 “Record the management review”: management sees the open points, each gets a person and a date, and management approves the documents. An assistant fills in nothing in 7.3.

12.4 “Detect attacks and prove it to the BSI”, only for operators of critical facilities: an assistant can enter the attack detection system and the day of the last evidence. The audit itself happens outside the walkthrough.
walk.seeItAlt: The activity log, day by day: who changed what and when, with names and times, and changes made through an assistant marked “via” and its name
walk.next: Build your records in the walkthrough

items.q: Do I have to disclose that an AI wrote the records?
items.a: We found no such duty in NIS 2 or the BSIG. The AI Act requires deployers to disclose AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest (Art. 50(4)); on our reading, internal records are not that. In the walkthrough it is visible anyway, through the mark and the log.

items.q: Will an auditor accept AI-generated policies?
items.a: We cannot predict that, and we know of no rule on it. What can be asked for is evidence that a policy is implemented. In the walkthrough, a document goes further only once a person has ticked “I have read the document, and it fits our company”.

items.q: How often is a company audited under NIS 2?
items.a: NIS 2 sets no fixed interval for everyone. For essential entities regular and targeted audits are possible; for important ones the authority acts after the fact. In Germany the BSI can order individual particularly important entities to have audits by independent bodies (§ 61(1) BSIG) and ask other particularly important entities for evidence at the earliest three years after the law entered into force (§ 61(3)). Operators of critical facilities give evidence every three years (§ 39).

items.q: Does an auditor see in the export what the assistant entered?
items.a: No. The export shows status, documents, registers and approvals with names and dates. Which entries came from an assistant is shown by the mark on the screen and the activity log. In the app, admins and people with the reviewer or legal reviewer role see the log.

meta.title: ChatGPT MCP connector for the NIS2 walkthrough
meta.description: Connect ChatGPT to the NIS2 walkthrough: add a custom MCP server, sign in through the browser, confirm each entry. What ChatGPT fills in, and what not.

chatgpt.title: Connecting ChatGPT to the NIS2 walkthrough
chatgpt.subtitle: In ChatGPT, go to Plugins, add a custom MCP server with the address https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp and sign in through the browser. According to OpenAI, ChatGPT cannot send a key. We have not tested this route ourselves yet; the steps follow OpenAI's documentation as of October 2026.

sections.heading: How do I add the walkthrough to ChatGPT?
paragraphs: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard an AI assistant uses to work with other software. The NIS 2 walkthrough offers an MCP server for it, and ChatGPT adds it as a custom server.
According to OpenAI, you open the Plugins page in ChatGPT, select the plus button, then "Add custom MCP server". Enter a name, for example nisd2, and under "Connection" the address below.

Then configure authentication, review the risk warning, confirm with "I understand and want to continue" and select "Create as a plugin". The labels are those in OpenAI's English documentation; your interface may word them differently.
Before that, an admin has to turn on "Allow AI assistants for this company" in the walkthrough's Settings. Your own account needs access to the walkthrough.

sections.heading: Signing in through the browser instead of a key
paragraphs: OpenAI states that ChatGPT cannot present custom API keys. The key you get in the walkthrough with "Create key" is therefore of no use in ChatGPT. You sign in through the browser instead, using OAuth: you allow access without giving ChatGPT your password.

In doing so, ChatGPT registers itself with the walkthrough's sign-in service. According to OpenAI, ChatGPT can use a Client ID Metadata Document or automatic registration (Dynamic Client Registration) for this. The walkthrough offers only automatic registration; if you are asked, choose that.

After you sign in, nisd2.eu shows which assistant is asking for which company and where the browser returns to afterwards. The return addresses OpenAI lists are on chatgpt.com. If the page shows anything else, click "Decline".
With "Allow", ChatGPT receives a token, a kind of pass with an expiry date. It lasts an hour and can be renewed, at most until 90 days after you allowed it. Then you allow ChatGPT again.

sections.heading: Does the server have to be reachable from the internet?
paragraphs: Yes, or through a tunnel. According to OpenAI the server needs a public https address or the Secure MCP Tunnel, because the requests come from OpenAI's network. nisd2.eu is reachable from the internet, so you need no tunnel there.

For a self-hosted instance inside the company network, OpenAI describes the tunnel like this: a small program called tunnel-client runs in your network and opens the connection outwards. It passes the requests on to the server.
Setting it up takes tunnel permissions in your OpenAI account. We have not tested the tunnel with the walkthrough.
Without a tunnel, software on your own computer, such as Claude Code, reaches an instance inside the company network directly.

sections.heading: What ChatGPT fills in, and what you confirm
paragraphs: ChatGPT reads the walkthrough and fills in what its items ask for, as you and with your rights. According to OpenAI, ChatGPT asks for your confirmation before write actions by default. The tool that fills in, fill_walkthrough_item, is marked as one that writes.

Before you confirm, read what ChatGPT is about to send: which item, which rows, which answers. A new answer replaces what the field held. According to OpenAI you can have ChatGPT remember your approval for a tool until the end of the conversation; it then stops asking in that conversation.
Upload evidence in the app. For a file, an assistant has to send its contents to storage itself; we have not tested whether ChatGPT can do that.
ChatGPT cannot finish, decide or sign anything, because the server has no tool for it. That stays with you, in the app.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: A good first task for ChatGPT is a list you already have.
points: 2.2 "Write down what your company has": give ChatGPT your inventory or a software list. It ticks on the four lists what appears in it and, on "Which software exactly, and from whom?", enters the provider.
A provider that is new there then appears on your supplier list in 5.1 "Write down who works for you". ChatGPT adds further suppliers there from your list of creditors.
Every screen ChatGPT wrote carries a mark with the assistant's name and the day. The activity log shows the change under your name, with "via" and the assistant's name.
Check each list, remove what is wrong in the app, and finish the item there.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect ChatGPT

items.q: Which ChatGPT plan can add custom MCP servers?
items.a: According to OpenAI, you add custom MCP servers in ChatGPT on the web, and your account and workspace policies apply. Which plans allow it is not stated on the pages we read. If "Add custom MCP server" is missing, check your plan or ask your ChatGPT workspace admin.

items.q: Does OpenAI see the data from our walkthrough?
items.a: What ChatGPT reads from the walkthrough goes to OpenAI. It reads what it fetches for your request, with your rights. Which terms apply to that data depends on your OpenAI account; we have not checked them for this article. Read them before you connect.

items.q: Can ChatGPT delete entries in the walkthrough?
items.a: ChatGPT does not delete a supplier, an asset or a training, because there is no tool for it. It can correct a row and replace an answer, and it saves the crypto list in 9.1 as a whole: an entry it leaves out drops off. You remove anything entered wrongly in the app.

items.q: ChatGPT does not show the server's tools. What now?
items.a: According to OpenAI, open the connection under Plugins and select "Refresh", and ChatGPT reloads the server's description. If ChatGPT gets a refusal, check that the switch in the walkthrough is still on and that your account has access to the walkthrough.

items.q: Can everyone on the team connect ChatGPT?
items.a: Yes, once the switch is on and their account has access to the walkthrough. Each person connects their own assistant and signs in themselves, and ChatGPT then works with that person's rights. In Settings each person sees their connections and ends each one with "Disconnect".

meta.title: Compliance MCP servers compared: read, write, approve
meta.description: GRC MCP servers from Vanta, Drata, Secureframe, Sprinto, Kertos, Cyberday and the NIS2 walkthrough: who reads, who writes, who switches the assistant on.

grcMcpComparison.title: Compliance and GRC MCP servers compared
grcMcpComparison.subtitle: Four of the six GRC platforms whose documentation we read in October 2026 let an AI assistant read and write over MCP. Kertos describes reading only, and at Cyberday it creates only documentation items. They differ in who switches access on, whether deleting is allowed and what stays with a person.

sections.heading: Which GRC platforms have an MCP server?
paragraphs: GRC stands for governance, risk and compliance: software in which a company keeps its risks, policies, suppliers and evidence, for example for ISO 27001 or its NIS 2 obligations. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard an AI assistant such as Claude or ChatGPT uses to work with such software.

Vanta, Drata, Secureframe, Sprinto, Kertos and Cyberday each describe an MCP server. All six name sign-in through OAuth, in the browser with the person's own account. Vanta, Drata, Sprinto and Kertos state that the assistant can do only what the person's role allows.
Secureframe and Sprinto also offer an API key. At Secureframe everyone except admins needs such a key, or the right to create one, even for OAuth.

We compare what the vendors themselves write, as of October 2026. We have not tested their servers, and we give no ranking. We describe the NIS 2 walkthrough's MCP server along the same questions, from its code.

sections.heading: May the assistant write and delete?
paragraphs: Vanta lists as write actions creating or updating a risk, updating an issue's status and uploading a policy document. In the privacy programme this includes deleting, for example processing activities. Drata has scopes for creating, updating and deleting; what can be deleted is evidence, risks and vendors.

Secureframe writes that its server can create, update and delete. Sprinto lists, among others, creating risks, policies, controls and vendors, updating policies and closing incidents. Its page says nothing about deleting.

Kertos describes a connection with read permission and names no write actions: the assistant sees exactly what the person's own Kertos user can see. Cyberday reads tasks, documentation items and events, and so far the assistant can create only documentation items there.

In the NIS 2 walkthrough the assistant fills in what the items ask for: fields, lists, the inventory, ratings, agreements and policy texts. It does not delete a supplier, an asset or a training. It does replace an answer, though, and it saves the crypto list as a whole, so an entry it leaves out drops off the list.

sections.heading: Who switches the assistant on?
paragraphs: At Sprinto an admin turns MCP on for the organisation; according to Sprinto, turning it off stops all of the organisation's MCP connections immediately. Cyberday writes that MCP access is disabled by default and an admin has to enable it explicitly.

At Drata an administrator sets which scopes are available over MCP at all. Each person gets the intersection of those scopes and their role. At Vanta, according to its help pages, any user can connect; a small set of tools is reserved for admins.

In the NIS 2 walkthrough the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" is off until an admin turns it on. It is checked on every call, and turning it off ends every connected assistant. The assistant of a person with the Reviewer role reads but fills in nothing.

sections.heading: What stays with a person?
paragraphs: Under Art. 20(1) NIS 2, management bodies approve the cybersecurity risk-management measures and oversee their implementation. In Germany, § 38(1) BSIG obliges management to implement the measures and oversee their implementation. Neither provision says whether an assistant may help.
Secureframe advises reviewing what the assistant is about to do before confirming, especially updates, deletes and archive actions. Drata advises admins to grant scopes that change data deliberately.

Sprinto lists among its MCP actions sending policies for approval or approving them. The assistant can also approve or reject steps in approval workflows there, as far as the person's role allows. We found no page from any of the vendors that excludes the assistant from approvals.

In the NIS 2 walkthrough the assistant finishes no item, decides none and signs nothing, because the server has no tool for it. The management review and the approval at item 7.3 exist only in the app.

sections.heading: How the NIS 2 walkthrough's MCP server is built
paragraphs: Its code is open, under the AGPL 3.0 licence. Every installation serves its MCP server at /api/mcp, including one on your own servers, and signs assistants in itself, with no third-party service.
Assistants sign in through the browser, using OAuth 2.1 with automatic registration, or with a key that lasts 90 days. Each person can make 300 calls an hour.

Cyberday writes that every action and data pull made through MCP is logged. In the walkthrough every change appears in the activity log under the person's name, with "via" and the assistant's name. Every screen an assistant wrote also carries a mark with its name and the day.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Two items show how the walkthrough separates filling in from approving.
points: 2.2 "Write down what your company has": the assistant ticks on the four lists what your inventory shows and enters which software exactly and from whom.
The screen then carries a mark such as "Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026". You check the list and finish the item in the app.
7.3 "Record the management review": the assistant fills in nothing here. A person records the management review in the app.
On "Management approves the documents", management approves, signed in with its own account.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 2.2, screen "Software for customers, staff and money". At the top the mark "Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026", below it the note that the entry "Warenwirtschaft (ERP)" is on your list.
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, connect your assistant

items.q: Which GRC MCP server is the best?
items.a: We give no ranking. Which one fits depends on whether your assistant should write, who switches it on and which steps you want to keep with a person. Check the vendor's current documentation; this comparison shows October 2026.

items.q: Is there an ISO 27001 MCP server?
items.a: Cyberday names ISO 27001 alongside NIS 2, DORA and the GDPR among its platform's frameworks. nisd2.eu is not an ISO 27001 certification tool: its MCP server works in the NIS 2 walkthrough. Our article on ISO 27001 MCP servers covers this in more detail.

items.q: Are there MCP servers that only provide knowledge about NIS 2?
items.a: Yes, for example NORMA from Kynosure: a collection covering eight frameworks, NIS 2 among them, with tools to search and map requirements, draft policies and run a gap analysis. Such servers hold no records of your company and fill none in.

items.q: Where is the data held, are there EU servers?
items.a: Vanta names a Europe region, Drata and Sprinto an EU address, Secureframe addresses in the US and the UK. That concerns the GRC platform. What the assistant reads also goes to the assistant's vendor, under your agreement with them. You can also run the NIS 2 walkthrough on your own servers.

meta.title: NIS2 Claude skill, connector or MCP server?
meta.description: A Claude skill carries knowledge about NIS2; a connector reaches your NIS2 walkthrough. What each one does, and when you need which of them.

claudeSkill.title: NIS2 Claude skill, connector or MCP server: which do you need?
claudeSkill.subtitle: A skill gives Claude instructions and knowledge for a task, such as NIS 2. A connector links Claude to another program; you add a custom one by the address of an MCP server. To read and fill in your NIS 2 walkthrough you connect its MCP server; your own skill can set out how Claude goes about it.

sections.heading: What is the difference between a skill, a connector and an MCP server?
paragraphs: According to Anthropic, a skill is a folder of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads when a task calls for it. At its core is a text file called SKILL.md with a name and a description of when Claude should use it.
An MCP server is a program's connection point for AI assistants. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard for it. The NIS 2 walkthrough has its MCP server at https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp.

According to Anthropic, a connector links Claude to an outside app or service, so Claude can find information there and take actions for you. You add a custom connector by the address of an MCP server. Anthropic sums up the difference like this: MCP connects Claude to external services and data sources, while skills provide the knowledge of how to complete a task.

sections.heading: What a NIS 2 skill can do, and what it cannot
paragraphs: A skill can explain to Claude what NIS 2 requires and set out how your company works: which lists it keeps, who is responsible for what, which terms it uses. It contains what someone wrote into it, and it goes out of date when the law or its transposition changes.
A skill brings no access to your data. Claude reads your progress in the walkthrough, your suppliers and your ratings through the MCP server.

Anthropic advises using skills only from trusted sources: ones you wrote yourself or got from Anthropic. A malicious skill can direct Claude to use tools or run code in ways that do not match its stated purpose. With the walkthrough connected, its tools are among them, so check a third-party NIS 2 skill file by file before you use it.

sections.heading: What the connector to the walkthrough does
paragraphs: Through the connector Claude reads your walkthrough: each item with its explanation, the provisions of the law it rests on and what your company has already entered. Then Claude fills in what the item asks for, as the person who connected it and with their rights.
Claude cannot finish, decide or sign anything there, because the server has no tool for it. That stays with you in the app, and the approval with management.
In Claude on the web and desktop you add a custom connector with the address and choose "Register automatically" for registration. In Claude Code you use the command below, then sign in with /mcp.
First an admin turns on "Allow AI assistants for this company" in Settings. We have tested Claude Code ourselves, Claude on the web not yet.
sections.code: claude mcp add --transport http nisd2 https://nisd2.eu/api/mcp

sections.heading: When do I need which?
paragraphs: You want to understand what NIS 2 requires, or have a text about the law drafted: a skill helps with that, without access to your data. Check the result against the text of the law.

You want to fill in your lists in the walkthrough, such as the inventory in 2.2: for that you connect the MCP server. Through it Claude enters data into your walkthrough, with a mark on every screen it wrote.

You can combine the two; that is our suggestion, and the walkthrough has no feature of its own for it. A skill your company writes itself sets out how Claude works with the connector, for example which list counts as the source for suppliers. The rule to leave open what your records do not show already comes with the server's instructions.
Do not put the key from Settings into a skill. It is your access for 90 days, in your name.

sections.heading: Where do I create a skill?
paragraphs: In Claude on the web, according to Anthropic, you upload a skill of your own as a ZIP file under "Customize", "Skills", via "+", "+ Create skill" and "Upload a skill". Code execution has to be on ("Code execution and file creation"). Check in your account whether your plan allows custom skills.

In Claude Code a skill is a folder with a SKILL.md, under ~/.claude/skills for yourself or under .claude/skills in the project. According to Anthropic, Claude Code picks up the skills from your Claude account when it is signed in with that account. Nothing syncs the other way or to the API; there you create a skill yourself.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: The first items show where a skill stops and the connector starts.
points: 2.1 "Decide how you rate risks": the item itself explains the method from BSI Standard 200-3, with a matrix and examples. Claude needs no skill for that; it reads the explanation through the connector.
On "Adopt the risk assessment method", Claude can adopt the method for your company through the connector, if that is what you want.

2.2 "Write down what your company has": with your inventory in the chat, Claude ticks on the four lists what applies to you and enters which software exactly it is and from whom. A skill of your own can set out which of your lists is the source.
Every screen Claude wrote shows the assistant's name and the day. You check the lists and finish the item in the app.
walk.seeItAlt: Settings in nisd2.eu with the switch "Allow AI assistants for this company" turned on, and below it the card "Connect assistants like Claude or Copilot" with the button "Create key"
walk.next: Start the walkthrough, add the connector

items.q: Is there a NIS 2 skill from nisd2.eu?
items.a: No, not as of October 2026. nisd2.eu offers an MCP server for the walkthrough, which you connect in Claude as a connector. What NIS 2 requires for an item is written in the walkthrough beside that item, and Claude reads it through the connector.

items.q: Can a skill enter anything into the walkthrough?
items.a: Not without the connector, because a skill brings no access to the walkthrough. It can tell Claude to use the tools of the connected server. The entry then goes through the connector, with your rights and with the mark on the screen.

items.q: Is a connector the same as an MCP server?
items.a: Nearly. The MCP server runs at the program, here in the walkthrough at /api/mcp. The connector is the entry in Claude that connects to it; in Claude Code the same entry is simply called an MCP server.

items.q: What does Anthropic see when Claude reads the walkthrough?
items.a: What Claude reads through the connector goes to Anthropic. For commercial products such as Claude for Work, Anthropic says it acts as a processor and does not use inputs and outputs for training by default. Personal accounts come with their own terms.

meta.title: GDPR compliance with an AI assistant and MCP: what works
meta.description: What an AI assistant can draft for the GDPR, what stays with the controller, and which lists from the NIS2 walkthrough help you get started.

gdprMcp.title: GDPR compliance with an AI assistant and MCP: what works, what does not
gdprMcp.subtitle: An AI assistant can draft GDPR records, such as entries in your record of processing activities, a description of your TOMs or a list of your processors. Your company, as controller, checks them and answers for them. nisd2.eu does not cover the GDPR, but lists from the NIS 2 walkthrough make useful source material.

sections.heading: Which GDPR records an AI assistant can draft
paragraphs: An AI assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot drafts from whatever you give it. Through MCP (Model Context Protocol), an open standard, it reads directly in programs that offer an MCP server, instead of you copying files into the chat.

The record of processing activities under Art. 30(1) GDPR contains, among other things, the purposes of the processing, the categories of data subjects and of personal data, and the categories of recipients. Where possible, it also holds erasure time limits and a general description of the technical and organisational measures (TOMs) under Art. 32. From a list of your processes and software, an assistant can lay out first entries.

It can compare a data processing agreement (DPA) with the points of Art. 28(3). These include instructions, confidentiality, the measures under Art. 32, and deletion or return at the end of the service.

It can structure a data protection impact assessment (DPIA), the assessment of a high-risk processing before it starts, along the minimum contents of Art. 35(7). From notes on a personal data breach it can prepare an entry with the facts, the effects and the remedial action, as Art. 33(5) requires.

sections.heading: What stays with the controller and the data protection officer
paragraphs: The controller is whoever determines the purposes and means of the processing (Art. 4(7) GDPR), which means your company. It is responsible for compliance with the principles in Art. 5(1) and must be able to demonstrate it (Art. 5(2)). A draft from an assistant changes none of that.

So your company decides whether measures are appropriate to the risk (Art. 32(1)). It chooses processors that provide sufficient guarantees (Art. 28(1)). It decides whether a processing needs a DPIA (Art. 35(1)) and whether a breach has to be notified (Art. 33(1)).

Where a data protection officer (DPO) is designated, they inform and advise, monitor compliance and give advice on the DPIA where requested (Art. 39(1)). An assistant can prepare work for them. The GDPR assigns the tasks themselves to the DPO.

sections.heading: What nisd2.eu does here, and what it does not
paragraphs: nisd2.eu helps with your NIS 2 obligations. It does not cover your GDPR obligations. The NIS 2 walkthrough keeps no record of processing activities, no TOMs under Art. 32 GDPR, no DPIA and no documentation of personal data breaches.

The nisd2.eu MCP server gives an assistant access to the walkthrough's 21 items, with the rights of the person who connected it. The assistant can also read items that are already finished or approved, in the areas assigned to that person. If an admin lets assistants read the records and the person may export, it also reads the company's records as the export holds them, incidents and training participants included.

The assistant writes the GDPR draft outside the walkthrough, as an answer in the chat or as a file. You file it wherever your company keeps its data protection records. The walkthrough has no screen for it.

sections.heading: Which walkthrough entries help
paragraphs: In 2.2 you record what your company does every day, such as “HR and payroll administration”, and which software you use from which vendor. In our reading, processing activities can be derived from these processes. Which personal data a process handles, however, is not on the list.

The list in 5.1 names each supplier with what it does for you. Whether it processes personal data on your behalf and is therefore a processor (Art. 4(8) GDPR) is not something the screen asks. You check that for each one.

The incident response plan in 3.1 says that if personal data is affected, you also notify the data protection authority unless a risk is unlikely (Art. 33 GDPR). The walkthrough has no place for the documentation under Art. 33(5).

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Three items of the walkthrough provide entries that whoever handles data protection at your company can work with.
points: 2.2 Write down what your company has: on “What your company does every day” an assistant ticks your processes, and on “Which software exactly, and from whom?” it enters the software and its vendors. You check each list and finish the item.

5.1 Write down who works for you: on “Your suppliers” it adds your suppliers, for example from your list of creditors. Which of them are processors you settle afterwards with whoever handles your data protection.

3.1 Plan what happens in an incident: under “Your emergency contacts” the walkthrough suggests, among others, the data protection officer as a contact, and “Your incident response plan” names the notification to the data protection authority. Management approves the plan in 7.3.
Every screen an assistant wrote shows its name and the day. That tells you what to check before you finish an item.
walk.seeItAlt: Item 2.2 of the NIS 2 walkthrough, screen “What your company does every day”: under “Business processes” 12 of 14 processes are ticked, such as “Sales and customer service”, “HR and payroll administration” and “Finance and accounting”
walk.next: Record your processes and software

items.q: Can ChatGPT or Claude create a record of processing activities?
items.a: A draft, yes. Art. 30(1) GDPR sets out what each entry contains. The assistant has to take purposes, recipients and erasure time limits from your records, and where they are missing it cannot know them. Have a person check every entry.

items.q: Do companies with fewer than 250 employees need a record of processing activities?
items.a: Art. 30(5) GDPR exempts organisations employing fewer than 250 persons unless the processing is likely to result in a risk to data subjects, is not occasional, or includes special categories of data or data relating to criminal convictions and offences. Check with whoever handles your data protection whether that applies to you.

items.q: Can AI carry out a data protection impact assessment?
items.a: The controller carries it out and seeks the advice of the DPO, where one is designated (Art. 35(1) and (2) GDPR). An assistant can structure the draft along Art. 35(7) and prepare questions. Your company assesses the risks and makes the decision.

items.q: Does NIS 2 software also take care of the GDPR?
items.a: nisd2.eu does not. The NIS 2 walkthrough records your NIS 2 obligations and refers to the GDPR in a few places, for example in the incident response plan in 3.1 and on supplier contracts in 5.2. No record of processing activities, TOMs or DPIA under the GDPR comes out of it.

items.q: MCP server and GDPR: where does the data the assistant reads go?
items.a: To the assistant's vendor, on the terms that apply to your account there. Our article on MCP server data protection explains this. For GDPR work it means: if you hand an assistant contracts or staff lists, its vendor processes that content too.

meta.title: GDPR TOMs with AI: drafting Art. 32 from NIS2 records
meta.description: An AI assistant reads your NIS2 walkthrough and drafts your Art. 32 GDPR TOMs from it. What fits, what is missing and what you check afterwards.

gdprToms.title: Drafting GDPR Art. 32 TOMs with AI from your NIS2 records
gdprToms.subtitle: An AI assistant can read your NIS 2 walkthrough and draft your TOMs under Art. 32 GDPR from it, in our mapping with encryption from 9.1, backups from 4.4 and emergency operation from 4.2. nisd2.eu does not cover the GDPR: the draft is your own document, which your company checks and completes.

sections.heading: What Art. 32 GDPR asks of your TOMs
paragraphs: TOMs are the technical and organisational measures you use to protect personal data. Art. 32(1) GDPR requires controllers and processors to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk for the rights and freedoms of natural persons. They take into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation, the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, and the varying likelihood and severity of the risk.

The measures include, in the words of the law, “inter alia as appropriate”. Point (a): “the pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data”. Point (b): “the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services”.

Point (c): “the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident”. Point (d): “a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures for ensuring the security of the processing”.

sections.heading: Which records in the NIS 2 walkthrough fit
paragraphs: The mapping below is our own; no supervisory authority has confirmed it. For point (a): 9.1 records your accepted methods and your cryptography policy, meaning what you encrypt with, where, and how you handle keys. The walkthrough contains nothing on pseudonymisation.

For point (b): the policy in 10.1 sets out who gets into what, who is bound to confidentiality, and what happens when someone leaves. 11.1 records where a second factor protects a sign-in, and 4.2 which processes must keep running without IT.
For point (c): 4.4 gives, for each backup system, how often it backs up and when a restore from it last worked. The business continuity plan in 4.2 says who restores the systems.

For point (d): the management review in 7.3 records when management looked at where things stand, who took part and what it decided. NIS 2 asks for procedures to assess the effectiveness of the measures (Art. 21(2)(f)).

sections.heading: What your NIS 2 records do not cover
paragraphs: Art. 21 NIS 2 protects network and information systems, whether or not they hold personal data. Art. 32 GDPR asks about the risk to the people whose data you process. Many measures serve both, but the question behind them differs.

The rating in 2.3 estimates how often something happens and how big the damage would be. The examples for it in 2.1 mean damage to the business, such as a day without shipping. The walkthrough does not explicitly ask about the risk to data subjects.
Also missing are pseudonymisation and the question of which measure applies to which processing. A draft from the walkthrough therefore covers only part of Art. 32, and your company adds the rest.

sections.heading: How an assistant writes the draft
paragraphs: An AI assistant connects to your company in nisd2.eu through MCP (Model Context Protocol), an open standard. With the get_walkthrough tool it reads the items in the areas assigned to the person who connected it, including finished and approved ones.

It writes the draft outside the walkthrough, as an answer in the chat or as a file. The document belongs to your company, and you file it wherever you keep your data protection records. The walkthrough has no screen for TOMs.
Have it back every statement with the item it comes from, and flag every gap. A request to the assistant can read like this:
sections.code: Use get_walkthrough to read items 9.1, 10.1, 11.1, 4.2, 4.4 and 7.3. From them, draft a description of our technical and organisational measures under Art. 32(1) GDPR, structured by points (a) to (d). For every statement, name the item it comes from. Flag every point for which the walkthrough contains nothing. Do not enter anything in the walkthrough.

sections.heading: What your company checks afterwards
paragraphs: Whether a measure is appropriate to the risk is for your company to decide as controller (Art. 32(1)). First check that every statement in the draft is true in your business. The walkthrough holds what people or an assistant entered.

Management's approval in 7.3 covers the walkthrough's NIS 2 documents. It does not approve your TOMs draft. Your company reviews that separately, with your data protection officer where one is designated.

If something later changes in the walkthrough, such as the date in 4.4 after a new restore test, the draft does not change with it. The GDPR requires measures to be reviewed and updated where necessary (Art. 24(1)).

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: Three items of the walkthrough record measures that an Art. 32 GDPR draft can draw on.
points: 9.1 Write the cryptography policy: “Your accepted methods” and “Your cryptography policy” say what you encrypt with and where. An assistant can fill in both. You read them and finish the item, and management approves the policy in 7.3.

4.4 Record your backups: on “Your backup systems” each system shows how often it backs up and when a restore last worked. After each restore test you enter the new date and carry it over into your TOMs.
4.2 Write the business continuity plan: “What must keep running” and “Your business continuity plan” record emergency operation and recovery. You read the plan and finish the item.

On the “Export” page, admins, reviewers and management open “Everything in one document” and save the complete documentation with “Save as PDF”. Pass it on with the draft to whoever handles your data protection.
walk.seeItAlt: The “Complete documentation” from the export, headed “NIS 2 documentation”, with a sample company's details, the contents from “Implementation status” to “Answers by area”, and the “Save as PDF” button at the top
walk.next: Record your backups in the walkthrough

items.q: Do NIS 2 measures automatically meet Art. 32 GDPR?
items.a: Not automatically. Art. 32 asks about the risk to the people whose data you process, and it names pseudonymisation, which the walkthrough does not cover. Many measures overlap, but for the GDPR you still check them one by one.

items.q: Do TOMs need a separate document?
items.a: Art. 32 does not prescribe one. The record of processing activities should, where possible, contain a general description of the measures under Art. 32(1) (Art. 30(1)(g)), and you must be able to demonstrate that processing complies with the GDPR (Art. 24(1)). Where you keep the description is something to settle with whoever handles your data protection.

items.q: Which TOMs apply to processors?
items.a: Art. 32(1) applies to processors too, and the contract with them must stipulate that they take all measures required under Art. 32 (Art. 28(3)(c)). In the walkthrough, 5.2 records for each supplier whether its contract settles security and incident reporting. The vendor's own TOMs are not recorded there.

items.q: Can ChatGPT write GDPR TOMs?
items.a: As a draft, yes. Without access to your records an assistant describes generic measures that need not be true in your business. Through MCP it reads what your company has recorded in the walkthrough instead. ChatGPT connects through the browser sign-in for this, which we have not tested ourselves yet.

meta.title: ISO 27001 MCP server: run an ISMS with an AI assistant
meta.description: What an AI assistant can keep up in an ISMS through an MCP server, what management and the certification body keep, and where the NIS 2 walkthrough helps.

iso27001.title: ISO 27001 MCP server: running an ISMS with an AI assistant
iso27001.subtitle: An ISO 27001 MCP server is the connection through which an AI assistant works inside the tool that holds your ISMS. It can keep the inventory, suppliers and risk register current and write drafts. The management review, accepting residual risks and the certificate stay with people. nisd2.eu is no certification tool: its server works in the NIS 2 walkthrough.

sections.heading: What is an ISO 27001 MCP server?
paragraphs: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It is an open standard that lets an AI assistant such as Claude or Copilot use another program: it reads data there and calls functions. An ISO 27001 MCP server is the MCP server of a tool in which a company runs its ISMS, its information security management system.

There are two kinds. A knowledge server answers questions about the standard and does not know your company. The server of your own tool reads your records and, depending on the vendor, writes to them too. Only the second kind takes work off your hands in your own lists.
The nisd2.eu MCP server is of the second kind. It works in the NIS 2 walkthrough, which does not run an ISO 27001 ISMS.

sections.heading: What can an AI assistant keep up in an ISMS?
paragraphs: ISO 27001 is paywalled. We give the standard's numbers, titles and content here as the nisd2.eu data model records them. The measures in the standard's Annex A are called controls there.

An assistant mostly keeps up lists whose facts already exist somewhere else. It compiles the inventory of information and other associated assets (control A.5.9) from an existing inventory list and your invoices. It reads the suppliers, and what their contracts settle on security (A.5.19 and A.5.20), from your accounts payable list and the contracts.

In the risk register (clauses 8.2 and 8.3) it proposes for each entry how often damage can occur and how large it would be. It drafts policies and a first version of the Statement of Applicability, which our data model places under risk treatment.
All of these are drafts. An assistant knows your company from what it may read and what you tell it. Whether an entry is right is checked by someone who knows the business.

sections.heading: What the standard leaves to management and risk owners
paragraphs: According to our data model, top management reviews the ISMS at planned intervals, looking at audit results, metrics, incidents and changes (management review, clause 9.3). Under clause 5.1 it approves the policy and provides the resources.
Under clause 6.1.3 the risk owners, the people accountable for a risk, approve the risk treatment plan and accept the residual risks.

NIS 2 starts with management: the management bodies approve the measures and oversee their implementation (Art. 20(1) NIS 2). For certain digital services, such as cloud and data centres, Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 is more specific. There the management bodies accept the risk assessment results and the residual risks, or accountable persons with the authority to manage risks who report to management (Annex point 2.1.1).
An assistant can gather the material for the management review. Reviewing, accepting and approving stay with the people the standard and the law name for it.

sections.heading: Who issues the ISO 27001 certificate?
paragraphs: A certification body, after an audit. In Germany the Deutsche Akkreditierungsstelle (DAkkS) accredits such bodies; it describes itself as the national accreditation body. A DAkkS accreditation annex for one certification body names ISO/IEC 17021-1 and ISO/IEC 27006-1 as the yardstick. The second sets the requirements for bodies that audit and certify information security management systems.

The database of accredited bodies on dakks.de shows whether a body is accredited for ISO 27001. Neither an assistant nor a tool replaces the audit, nisd2.eu included: it takes you through your NIS 2 obligations.

sections.heading: Where the NIS 2 walkthrough and ISO 27001 overlap
sections.law: ENISA mapping table v1.2 · Annex CIR 2024/2690
paragraphs: In a table (version 1.2 of 21 August 2025), ENISA, the EU's cybersecurity agency, maps each point in the Annex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 to parts of ISO 27001:2022. The asset inventory (Annex point 12.4) to A.5.9, for example, the risk management framework (point 2.1) to 6.1.3, 8.2 and 8.3 among others, and the effectiveness of measures (point 7.1) to 9.3 among others.

On its cover page ENISA writes that the table “should not be interpreted as a measure of equivalency among different standards or frameworks”. It names relevant requirements “without assessing whether these fully cover the requirements of the regulation”.

Our mapping in the nisd2.eu data model sets the walkthrough items beside them: 2.2 to A.5.9, 2.3 to 8.2 and 8.3, 5.2 to A.5.20, 6.3 to A.8.8, 4.4 to A.8.13 and 7.3 to 9.3. It is our reading, not a statement by any certification body. For an ISO 27001 project these lists are a start.

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: The lists an ISMS builds on come together in the walkthrough at 2.2 and 2.3; at 7.3 management sees the risk map drawn from them.
points: 2.2 Write down what your company has: the assistant ticks what your inventory shows and, under “Which software exactly, and from whom?”, enters the product and its provider. You check the list and finish 2.2.

2.3 Rate your risks: on “Rate your software”, “Rate your technology and rooms” and “Rate your suppliers” it proposes how often and how much damage. The app works out the map “Your risks at a glance” from that, and there you change whatever does not fit.
7.3 Record the management review: no assistant fills in anything here. A person enters the review, and management approves the documents, signed in with its own account.
Every screen an assistant wrote shows its name and the day, such as “Filled in by the assistant claude-code/2.1.287 on 16 October 2026”.
walk.seeItAlt: Walkthrough item 2.3, screen “Your risks at a glance”: a matrix of “How often it happens” (from rare to very often) against “How big the damage would be” (from negligible to existential), each field showing the number of entries and their level from low to very high.

items.q: Can AI create the ISO 27001 Statement of Applicability?
items.a: A draft, yes. Our data model places the Statement of Applicability under risk treatment (clause 8.3), and an assistant can derive a first version from your risk register. People decide how you treat your risks, and the statement depends on that.

items.q: Do auditors accept ISO 27001 documents written by AI?
items.a: We have found no rule on it, as far as we could check (October 2026), so we cannot say whether an auditor accepts such documents. ComplianceForge, a vendor of templates and so not neutral, writes that auditors compare documentation to reality. So check above all that your business does what the text says.

items.q: Is ISO 27001 mandatory for NIS 2?
items.a: The NIS 2 Directive does not require an ISO 27001 certificate. It asks for the measures to take into account the state of the art and, where applicable, relevant European and international standards (Art. 21(1)). Member States encourage the use of such standards (Art. 25).

items.q: Does the NIS 2 walkthrough replace an ISO 27001 ISMS?
items.a: No. The walkthrough records what your NIS 2 obligations require and ends with management's approval at 7.3. A Statement of Applicability, an internal audit programme and certification are not part of it. You can reuse its lists and documents for an ISMS.

items.q: Which ISMS tools have an MCP server?
items.a: Several vendors of governance, risk and compliance tools offer MCP servers, with different rights to read, write and delete. Our comparison of compliance MCP servers sets them side by side, as of October 2026. Check for each whether an assistant may also approve or delete.

meta.title: Cyber Resilience Act with an AI assistant: SBOM and reports
meta.description: What an AI assistant can take off a manufacturer's plate under the Cyber Resilience Act, what the manufacturer decides, and what buyers record in NIS 2.

cra.title: Cyber Resilience Act with AI: what an MCP server can do for manufacturers
cra.subtitle: Since 11 September 2026 the Cyber Resilience Act has obliged manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents; from 11 December 2027 they must also keep a list of software components (SBOM). An AI assistant can maintain the SBOM and draft reports. The manufacturer decides whether to report. The nisd2.eu MCP server serves buyers, in the NIS 2 walkthrough.

sections.heading: What does the Cyber Resilience Act require of manufacturers?
sections.law: Art. 3(1), (2) and (13), Art. 13(8), Annex I Part II CRA
paragraphs: The Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, covers products with digital elements: software and hardware, together with the data processing at a distance that the manufacturer develops for them and without which the product could not perform one of its functions (Art. 3(1) and (2)).

Its duties fall mainly on the manufacturer. That is whoever develops or manufactures such products, or has them developed or manufactured, and markets them under its own name or trademark (Art. 3(13)). One example is a company that sells its own software or a connected device.

For vulnerability handling, Annex I Part II lists eight duties, among them: document components and vulnerabilities, remediate without delay, disclose fixed vulnerabilities and give a contact address for reports. This holds for the support period, as a rule at least five years (Art. 13(8)).

sections.heading: What is an SBOM under the CRA, and who gets it?
sections.law: Art. 3(39), Art. 13(13) and (24), Annex I Part II(1), Annex II(9), Annex VII CRA
paragraphs: The SBOM (software bill of materials) is a formal record of the components in a product's software and their supply chain relationships (Art. 3(39)). The manufacturer draws it up in a commonly used, machine-readable format covering at the very least the top-level dependencies (Annex I Part II(1)).

The Regulation names no particular format; the Commission may set the format and elements by implementing acts (Art. 13(24)). The SBOM is part of the technical documentation, which the manufacturer keeps available for at least ten years (Art. 13(13), Annex VII).

The manufacturer does not have to publish it. Whether users get it is the manufacturer's choice (Annex II(9)). A market surveillance authority receives it on a reasoned request, where it needs it to check compliance (Annex VII(8)).

sections.heading: Which reporting deadlines apply since 11 September 2026?
paragraphs: Manufacturers report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting the security of the product, including for products already on the market before 11 December 2027 (Art. 69(3)). A vulnerability is actively exploited when there is reliable evidence that a malicious actor has exploited it in a system without the owner's permission (Art. 3(42)).

For a vulnerability: an early warning within 24 hours of the manufacturer becoming aware of it and a notification within 72 hours. The final report follows no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available. For an incident the same 24 and 72 hours apply, and the final report follows within one month of the notification.

Reports go through ENISA's single reporting platform, simultaneously to the CSIRT designated as coordinator and to ENISA (Art. 14(1) and (7), Art. 16). A CSIRT is a computer security incident response team designated by a Member State; as a rule it is the one in the country of the manufacturer's main establishment. The manufacturer also informs the impacted users (Art. 14(8)).

sections.heading: What an AI assistant can do for manufacturers
paragraphs: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an AI assistant such as Claude or Copilot use another program. An MCP server is a program's connection for it. For the work below the assistant needs access to your development tools, for example through their MCP servers where the vendor offers one.

An assistant that works in the place where your source code is kept (the code repository) can have the SBOM generated for every new version and check that it matches what you ship. Our course “CRA SBOM Fundamentals” shows which formats exist and which tools generate an SBOM.

It matches the SBOM against published vulnerabilities, for example in ENISA's European vulnerability database, and prepares the hits for a person. It drafts the notes on fixed vulnerabilities (Annex I Part II(4)) and the message to the maintainer of an affected component (Art. 13(6)).
For a report it prepares what Art. 14(2) lists: the product concerned, the nature of the exploit, the measures taken and what users can do themselves.

sections.heading: What the manufacturer decides itself
sections.law: Art. 3(31), Art. 13(8), Art. 28(1) and (4), Annex I Part II(4) CRA
paragraphs: The Regulation addresses these duties to the manufacturer. It does not say who in the company decides.

The EU declaration of conformity, a document the manufacturer draws up, states that meeting the requirements of Annex I has been demonstrated. With it the manufacturer assumes responsibility for its product (Art. 28(1) and (4)). With the CE marking on the product it indicates that the product and its processes meet those requirements (Art. 3(31)).

Several steps are judgements: whether the evidence of exploitation is reliable, how long the support period is, and whether information on a fixed vulnerability is published later in duly justified cases. An assistant supplies the material. We recommend that a person who may act for the manufacturer decides.

sections.heading: What nisd2.eu covers here
sections.law: Art. 21(2)(e) NIS 2 · Art. 13(19), Annex II(2) CRA
paragraphs: The nisd2.eu MCP server fills in only the NIS 2 walkthrough; once an admin allows it, it also reads the company's records for someone who may export, the vulnerability and patch registers included. It keeps no SBOM, reports nothing to ENISA and records no CRA obligations.

It helps on the buyer's side. NIS 2 requires security when you acquire your IT, including vulnerability handling (Art. 21(2)(e)). The CRA gives you facts to ask for. For products placed on the market from 11 December 2027, the manufacturer states the end of the support period at the time of purchase, at least month and year (Art. 13(19)). The product also comes with a point of contact for reporting vulnerabilities (Annex II(2)).

walk.heading: How the walkthrough does it
walk.lead: In the NIS 2 walkthrough you are on the buyer's side: you record what you require of manufacturers and suppliers.
points: 6.3 Write the rules for buying, updates and vulnerabilities: the section “When buying” already says you check whether and for how long a provider supplies security updates. An assistant can add under “Further rules” that you ask for the end of the support period. You read the rules; management approves them at the end of the walkthrough.
5.2 Record what you have agreed with your suppliers: it ticks for each supplier whether the contract settles security requirements and reporting incidents to you. You check each row.
2.2 Write down what your company has: the list names each program with its provider. It lets you see which vulnerability notices concern you; 6.3 shows where such notices appear.

7.3 Record the management review: a supplier rated high or very high risk whose contract settles neither security nor incidents appears under “What the answers still leave open”. There you set who takes care of it and by when.
walk.seeItAlt: The start page of the NIS 2 walkthrough, with “Your path” on the right listing the items in order, starting with “Register with your authority”, the first three ticked.

items.q: When does the Cyber Resilience Act apply?
items.a: The Regulation has been in force since 10 December 2024. The reporting obligations in Art. 14 have applied since 11 September 2026, the rules on notifying the bodies that assess products (Chapter IV) since 11 June 2026, and everything else applies from 11 December 2027 (Art. 71(2)).

items.q: Does the CRA apply to software as a service?
items.a: Only where a cloud solution is a product's data processing at a distance, such as controlling a smart home device remotely. Cloud services designed and developed outside the responsibility of a product's manufacturer are not covered by the CRA. Recital 12 places software as a service under the NIS 2 Directive, for providers of medium size and above.

items.q: Does the CRA affect companies that only buy software?
items.a: The duties lie mainly with manufacturers, authorised representatives, importers and distributors. Anyone who substantially modifies a product and makes it available on the market counts as its manufacturer (Art. 22(1)). In our reading, a company that only buys and uses software has no CRA duties of its own.

items.q: Can AI submit the CRA report to ENISA?
items.a: The Regulation does not say who in the company reports. It obliges the manufacturer, and the early warning is due within 24 hours. We recommend that an assistant prepares the draft and a person checks and submits it.

items.q: How do the CRA and NIS 2 relate?
items.a: NIS 2 governs the cybersecurity of entities, the CRA that of products; for the term incident, the CRA refers to NIS 2 (Art. 3(43)). If a NIS 2 company is itself a manufacturer, both apply. If it buys products, the CRA's information helps it with its supply chain.
